text:
“Mama, we did it!”

Her mother cried as she held her daughter.

“Yes, my child. We did it.”

While other graduates celebrated with expensive gifts and parties, Nadia and her mother returned home to eat a modest meal of rice and stew.

But for them, that meal tasted better than any expensive dinner in the world.

They had survived.

And their story was only beginning.

After graduation, Nadia applied for dozens of jobs.

She attended interviews, submitted applications, and waited for phone calls that never came.

Eventually, she secured a job as an assistant at a small clothing company.

Her salary was modest, but she was grateful.

Nadia worked harder than everyone else. She arrived early, stayed late, and studied everything she could about the business.

She noticed that the company wasted money on poor marketing and failed to understand what customers wanted.

One evening, she prepared a detailed proposal showing how the company could attract more customers through affordable clothing, better designs, and online advertising.

She presented it to her manager.

He glanced at the document and laughed.

“Who asked you to teach us how to run a business?”

“I only wanted to help the company grow, sir.”

“Then concentrate on your job. You are an assistant, not a business expert.”

He threw the proposal onto his desk.

Nadia picked it up and walked away.

That night, she cried again.

But this time, she did not cry because someone had insulted her. She cried because she had finally realized that some people would rather watch you remain small than admit that you have something valuable to offer.

Instead of giving up on her idea, Nadia started researching the clothing industry in her spare time.

She saved a portion of every salary she received.

She learned about fabrics, suppliers, customer service, branding, and online sales.

After three years, she had saved enough money to rent a tiny shop.

She resigned from her job and opened a small clothing business.

Her mother was frightened.

“Nadia, what if this business fails? We don’t have money to start again.”

Nadia held her mother’s hands.

“Mama, I would rather try and fail than spend the rest of my life wondering what could have happened if I had tried.”

Her mother eventually gave her blessing.

Nadia named the business Nadia Styles.

At first, customers barely entered the shop.

Some days, she sold nothing.

She sat alone, staring at the clothes hanging on the racks, wondering whether she had made a terrible mistake.

But she refused to close the shop.

She began posting pictures of her designs online. She offered affordable prices, treated every customer with respect, and made sure every order was delivered properly.

Slowly, things began to change.

One customer recommended her to another.

A popular fashion influencer purchased one of her outfits and posted it online.

Within days, Nadia received more orders than she could handle.

She hired two workers.

Then five.

Then ten.

Within two years, her little shop became a recognized clothing brand.

She opened branches in other cities and eventually began supplying clothing to major retailers….

🟧 SNF PULSE — WASHINGTON JUST CHANGED THE ENERGY SANCTIONS CALCULATION.

While oil markets confront escalating Middle East supply risks, the White House has made a consequential policy decision.

President Trump signed an executive order waiving key provisions of the new Russia sanctions law before additional penalties were scheduled to take effect October 18.

The waived measures include proposed 100% tariffs targeting certain major purchasers of Russian oil and gas.

Existing Russia sanctions remain in place.

🟨 THE STORY ISN'T JUST RUSSIA.

It's the growing conflict between geopolitical pressure and energy affordability.

Washington is attempting to manage two competing objectives:

Maintain economic pressure on Russia while preventing additional disruptions to global energy supply.

The waiver reduces the immediate threat of another sanctions-driven trade shock.

But it doesn't resolve the underlying energy crisis.

🟨 WHAT THE MARKET IS PRICING IN

Oil markets are already confronting security threats across the Middle East, pressure on shipping routes and increasingly complicated supply relationships.

Additional restrictions on Russian energy could have introduced another layer of uncertainty.

The waiver changes that calculation.

The important distinction: avoiding new penalties is not the same as delivering additional physical supply.

Energy markets still need evidence that available barrels can reach buyers efficiently.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

Whether Russian energy exports increase measurably.

How major importing countries respond to the waiver.

Whether refined-product availability improves.

And whether any improvement in energy supply begins reducing inflation expectations and pressure on global bond markets.

SNF LENS

🟠 Signal: Washington waives new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs before implementation.

⚪ Noise: Assuming the decision immediately lowers oil prices or eliminates existing restrictions.

🟢 Confirmation: Observable export flows, improved product availability and reduced energy-market stress.

🔴 Risk: Further Middle East disruptions overwhelm the relief offered by the sanctions waiver.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

Energy policy is becoming an increasingly important instrument of macroeconomic stabilization.

But sanctions relief cannot replace physical supply.

The market must now determine whether Washington's policy adjustment translates into actual energy availability, or simply removes one additional source of uncertainty.

For the Fed, the bond market and global equities, that distinction matters.

text:
Estados Unidos ofrece otros 17 millones de barriles de reservas estratégicas de petróleo a medida que se agrava la crisis del combustible.
Por Julianne Geiger - 16 de octubre de 2026, 13:30 CDT

Estados Unidos pondrá a la venta otros 17 millones de barriles de crudo de la Reserva Estratégica de Petróleo, un día después de que la AIE acelerara la liberación de reservas de emergencia, mientras los gobiernos se apresuran a introducir más petróleo y combustible en un mercado saturado.

El Departamento de Energía emitió el viernes una solicitud de propuestas para un intercambio de hasta 17 millones de barriles, parte de los 172 millones de barriles que Washington se comprometió a poner a disposición en virtud de la medida de emergencia de 400 millones de barriles anunciada en marzo por la AIE.

Actualmente, la Reserva Estratégica de Petróleo (SPR, por sus siglas en inglés) cuenta con unos 283 millones de barriles. Si las empresas extraen los 17 millones de barriles completos antes de que se realicen los reembolsos, las existencias se reducirían a aproximadamente 266 millones de barriles, lo que se sitúa justo dentro del rango de 250 a 300 millones de barriles que generalmente se considera la zona mínima operativa de la reserva.

Hay un inconveniente bastante importante: alguien tiene que querer el petróleo.

El Departamento de Energía ofreció en junio la última parte de su compromiso de marzo, exigiendo a las empresas que devolvieran el crudo prestado posteriormente con primas de hasta el 24%. Las empresas acordaron aceptar solo unos 500.000 barriles.

El gobierno lo está intentando de nuevo. El API estimó que las reservas de crudo de EE. UU. cayeron 11,12 millones de barriles la semana pasada, tras un descenso de 2,09 millones de barriles la semana anterior. Los inventarios comerciales han perdido más de 51 millones de barriles en las últimas 26 semanas.

La solicitud del viernes se produce tras una nueva escalada en la campaña de reservas de emergencia. La AIE anunció el jueves que sus miembros acelerarían la entrega de los aproximadamente 100 millones de barriles pendientes desde marzo, incluidos más de 20 millones de barriles de diésel, lo antes posible.

Washington está ofreciendo ahora 17 millones de barriles más, con una reserva estratégica de reservas (SPR) de 283 millones de barriles en un mercado que ya demostró este verano que endeudarse con el gobierno para obtener crudo con condiciones de pago costosas no es necesariamente un acuerdo que las refinerías deseen.

text:
I want to thank Marc Gendron for important message in the Post-Star. A candidate refusing to debate is like an applicant refusing to show up to a job interview: it's disqualifying, and raises more questions than it answers. 
---
Why I’m voting for Constantino
If you want a job, you show up for the interview. That's true for a line cook, a welder, or a schoolteacher, and it should be true for anyone asking to represent us in Congress.

Anthony Constantino understands that: that’s why he accepted all six dates offered by CBS6 for the debate, which was broadcast to every member of our communities. He was willing to stand in front of voters, take tough questions, and defend his record and his ideas in the open.
Blake Gendebien accepted none. Not one. The man asking us to trust him with a seat in Congress wouldn't spend a single evening answering questions alongside his opponent. What exactly was he afraid of?
Whatever the reason, the result is the same. Upstate voters are being asked to hire someone who refused to sit for the interview.

In a district as large as ours, stretching across hundreds of miles of small towns and rural roads, many voters will never meet the candidates in person. A televised debate is one of the only chances we get to see them side-by-side and judge for ourselves. By dodging every one, Gendebien told us he'd rather run on ads and talking points than face scrutiny. 

A congressman's whole job is to speak up for us when it's hard, to argue our case in rooms full of people who disagree. If Gendebien wouldn't defend himself in front of his own future constituents, how can we expect him to stand up for us in Washington?

Constantino was ready to make his case. Gendebien was hiding from his.
That’s why I’m voting for Anthony Constantino.

Marc Gendron
Plattsburgh

text:
AMERICA WAS ONCE THE LEADER OF THE FREE WORLD. WHAT HAPPENED?

Not long ago, the United States was the undisputed leader of the democratic world, a defender of international law, and a country whose promises carried enormous weight. American leadership inspired confidence among allies and forced aggressors to consider the consequences of their actions.

That began to change in 2014, when Russia invaded Ukraine and illegally annexed Crimea. President Barack Obama responded with sanctions and diplomatic pressure, but Washington failed to stop Russian aggression. This was particularly troubling because the United States had signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, providing security assurances to Ukraine in exchange for surrendering its nuclear arsenal.

The United Nations also demonstrated its weakness. With Russia holding veto power in the Security Council, the organization proved incapable of enforcing international law against a permanent member.

Compare this with Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990. The United States assembled an international coalition, defeated the aggressor, and restored Kuwait's sovereignty. American leadership was decisive. When Ukraine faced Russian aggression, however, Washington chose a fundamentally different approach.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, President Joe Biden initially acted with extreme caution. Washington offered Volodymyr Zelenskyy assistance with evacuation, but Ukraine's president refused to leave his country.

American military assistance eventually became essential to Ukraine's survival. Yet the Biden administration repeatedly delayed weapons deliveries, restricted their use, and appeared more concerned about Russian escalation than Ukrainian victory. In my opinion, Washington provided enough assistance to prevent Ukraine's defeat, but not enough to ensure Russia's defeat.

Instead of delivering peace, Trump became involved in another major conflict, this time with Iran, contributing to instability in the Persian Gulf, rising energy prices, and growing international economic uncertainty.

And somehow, Trump increasingly directs his anger toward Ukraine and President Zelenskyy rather than Vladimir Putin, the man responsible for invading Ukraine.

Meanwhile, America's relationships with its closest allies have deteriorated. Canada and the European Union, partners that stood beside Washington for generations, now face an American administration that frequently treats them more like competitors than friends.

Trump's approach to Russia is even more disturbing. His statements and decisions repeatedly raise questions about whether Washington still recognizes the fundamental difference between an aggressor and a country fighting for its survival.

How can Trump promise to make America great again while undermining the very alliances and international institutions that helped establish American greatness?

But blaming Trump alone would be unfair.

America's declining international credibility did not begin with his presidency. Under Obama, Biden, and Trump, Washington repeatedly demonstrated a growing unwillingness to match its declarations about democracy and international law with decisive action.

The consequences have accumulated over more than a decade.

For generations, America's greatest strength was never simply its military power, nuclear arsenal, or economic influence. It was the belief that the United States stood for something greater: freedom, democracy, sovereignty, and a rules-based international order.

That belief has been seriously damaged.

Nobody knows exactly what awaits America or the rest of the world. But I am convinced of one thing: the United States will never simply return to the international position it once occupied.

The world has fundamentally changed. Traditional alliances are being tested, global power is shifting, and humanity is approaching a period of profound political, economic, and social transformation.

text:
On the temporary prohibition question, I think we already have it. Chapter 27 lets a court order involuntary hospitalization for substance use disorder after an examination and a hearing with counsel, on a finding that the person has "lost the power of self-control" — nearly the words of an 1874 Connecticut statute. Anyone committed that way is already disarmed by subdivision (4). That's the drinker the history reaches, and he gets a hearing first. Subdivision (2) reaches a much larger group with no hearing at all.

On renunciation, the loyalist laws are the best analogue anyone has offered, and I think they fail on one detail. Those were wartime measures aimed at people who refused an oath they remained free to take at any time. Section 922(g)(7) offers no oath and no way back.

I've got a longer piece on this coming. Would value your eyes on it first if you're willing. It’s for my Greenbrier Street Brief Substack which goes to various West Virginia policymakers.

text:
Daily Digest ⋆ Conservative & Center-Right Reporting

CURRENT HEADLINES 🛰️

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

Saturday, October 17, 2026 ⋆ 7:30 PM EDT (reporting cutoff)

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

Domestic U.S. ⋆ International ⋆ Science & Health ⋆ National Security ⋆ Unusual / underreported / America First-relevant.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

“In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act.” ~ George Orwell

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

This digest tracks the day’s consequential U.S. and world developments through a conservative and center-right lens, with a focus on American interests, security and the cost of living. Confirmed facts are kept apart from allegations, official claims and analysis, and contested claims are attributed to whoever makes them. Markets are closed for the weekend, so all figures are Friday’s closes.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

DOMESTIC U.S. NEWS 🦅

Bend, Oregon school shooting: three children and a teacher dead; gunman was a 16-year-old former student

Police say the 16-year-old, a former Silver Rail Elementary student, killed three children (ages 5, 8 and 11) and a 25-year-old teacher on Thursday. A bystander who legally owned the pistol shot him dead. Early “five dead” reports counted the shooter. Law enforcement sources told CBS the shotgun was bought by the suspect’s mother. No motive has been announced, and investigators are in the early stages of reviewing his devices and online activity. A 7-year-old girl is in serious but stable condition, and a wounded 54-year-old teacher is expected to survive. Police credited a teacher who tackled the gunman with preventing more bloodshed.
 Source: CBS News (updated Oct. 16, 10:24 PM EDT); KPTV/Gray News. Oregon school shooter identified, used shotgun bought by mother, sources say +2

“No Kings” holds “Vote Early” events today as early voting expands

The left-leaning coalition says today’s events aim to drive early turnout and build an election-protection volunteer network. A White House spokeswoman joked the group should change its name. Georgia officials report more than 180,000 ballots cast on the first day of early voting, a midterm record. North Carolina’s early voting began Thursday. USPS says it will take “extraordinary measures” on ballot delivery starting Oct. 24. Turnout for today’s events had not been reported by the cutoff. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Source: Fox News live coverage (Oct. 15–16), citing USA Today, AP and Reuters. Fox NewsFox News

DOJ sues California over alleged 20,000+ noncitizens on voter rolls

The Justice Department and DHS filed a complaint Thursday. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Homeland Security Investigations compared public voter files with federal immigration data to flag likely noncitizen registrants. Federal prosecutor Bill Essayli said California officials were given the chance to remove names and sequester ballots and refused. These are allegations, and no court has ruled. California’s response was not found in the reporting reviewed.

Source: Fox News. Fox News

Federal probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar widens
Authorities searched Omar’s Washington home under a “judicially authorized search” and subpoenaed some relatives in an investigation tied to her immigration to the U.S. Mullin has suggested it involves possible fraud on her family’s immigration paperwork. The warrant and filings are sealed, and DOJ and DHS have not detailed what was seized. CBS headlines this week also report Mullin calling it a “strong case.” Omar’s office calls the search an abuse of power. She has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. No charges have been announced.

Source: TNND/Scripps; CBS News. Investigation into Ilhan Omar intensifies after home searched, subpoenas issued +2

Press secretary Katie Zacharia “transitioning out” after one week

Zacharia was named Oct. 9 and held one 14-minute briefing on Oct. 13, taking three questions. On Friday President Trump told reporters he advised her to “reconsider,” and a senior White House official said she is transitioning out. Trump denied firing her. She acknowledged on Hannity that she never passed a bar exam or held a U.S. law license, despite Trump describing her as an attorney. Fox’s headline says she is “out,” but its body text says she is transitioning, so formal details are unconfirmed.

Source: Fox News. Fox News

Trump: Nidal Hasan’s execution will go ahead Dec. 3 but will not be streamed

Trump reversed an administration plan to livestream the Fort Hood shooter’s firing-squad execution. The Army has set it for Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. at Fort Hood, after Trump approved the death sentence. It would be the first U.S. military execution in more than 65 years. Hasan may seek federal court intervention, and the Army has not detailed its procedures.

Source: TNND/Scripps. newschannel9

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS 🌐

Hormuz ship attacks hit a weekly record as U.S. and Iran dispute whether the strait is open

The UKMTO says at least 10 vessels have been attacked in or near the strait since last Sunday, the most in any week of the war. There have been 23 attacks since Oct. 1, nearly double the average. Most ships now decline to report attacks, so the real count may be higher. Iran’s Guards said Saturday that a supertanker carrying over 2 million barrels hit a mine and caught fire, which is Tehran’s claim, with the location unspecified. The Trump administration insists the strait is open, while Tehran says it is closed without Iranian permission. Mediators are still passing messages. Iran wants the collapsed June memorandum restored, and no breakthrough is expected before the Nov. 3 U.S. vote or Israel’s Oct. 27 election.

Source: CBS News/AP/AFP; Al Jazeera (Oct. 11). CBS NewsAl Jazeera

Houthi–Saudi fighting widens; Egypt says it is ready to defend the kingdom

Saudi Arabia intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait and a drone fired at Riyadh early Sunday local time. At least 19 people have died in over a week of Houthi attacks, including 13 at Riyadh’s airport. Houthi missiles hit Aden’s airport Friday night with no casualties reported. A Thursday attack near Yemen’s government palace compound killed at least five. Houthi media claim Saudi strikes killed at least 12 on Saturday, which is unverified. Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging the group, and Iran denies involvement and offers to mediate. Egypt’s president said Cairo would defend Saudi Arabia “if requested,” pending parliamentary approval.

 Source: CBS News/AP/AFP. CBS News

Russian diesel deal and disputed “energy ceasefire” strain U.S.–Ukraine ties

Trump announced the diesel deal Oct. 9, and Treasury moved to ease diesel sanctions for six months, the first such license longer than the usual 30 days. Trump said Russia would supply over 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 in November and 1 million after that, with 3 million more later. Trump then declared an “energy ceasefire,” but Zelensky said Russia kept striking Ukrainian energy sites. Both parties have criticized the deal. Trump blamed Zelensky for high U.S. diesel costs and said he should step aside, which Zelensky has no intention of doing. Ukrainska Pravda, citing Axios, reports that envoys threatened to curb intelligence sharing over Ukraine’s refinery strikes. I have not independently verified this.

 Source: PBS/AP; Axios; Ukrainska Pravda. Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russian diesel in sharp reversal of U.S. policy ahead of midterms +4

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

BUSINESS & MARKETS 💹

Wall Street ends its worst week since June on AI-financing worries

On Friday the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659.44 and the Nasdaq sank 2.1%. For the week the S&P lost 1.9%, the Nasdaq 4.5% and the Dow gained 0.7%. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8%. The Dow slipped 0.3% to 52,002.41 (Nasdaq 26,140.03). Concerns about debt-funded AI buildouts weighed on tech, with CoreWeave down nearly 12%. Oil reversed higher, with Brent settling near $110 and WTI near $102.

Source: AP; Bloomberg-based market summaries. How major US stock indexes fared Friday 10/16/2026 - ABC News +3

September inflation runs hotter; gasoline near $4.33
Headline CPI rose 0.6% for the month and 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% economists expected. Core CPI rose 0.3% and 2.6% year over year. AAA puts regular gasoline at about $4.33, versus roughly $3.08 a year earlier. The Fed meets Oct. 28, and the first Q3 GDP estimate comes Oct. 29. The Atlanta Fed’s tracker shows 3.6% growth, but the average analyst estimate is well below 3%.

Source: CNBC; Charles Schwab. CNBCschwab

Analysts: Russian diesel deal unlikely to move prices

Experts told CNBC the deal gives Moscow only marginal revenue and won’t shift global prices much. One estimate puts the initial 1.8 million-ton tranche at up to $1.25 billion in extra export revenue over three months, but under $30 million a month for Russia’s federal budget.

Source: CNBC (Oct. 17). CNBC

Iraq says the Hormuz disruption has cost it about $60 billion

Iraq’s foreign minister said Thursday that the war has cost his country about $60 billion. Its exports were about 3.5 million barrels a day before the war and 2.6 million between Sept. 1 and 21. Foreign currency reserves are down $20 billion, according to Iraqi statements.

Source: CBS News/AFP. CBS News

Week ahead: earnings and Q3 GDP

Schwab’s calendar lists GE Aerospace, RTX, 3M, GM, Northrop Grumman, Halliburton, Netflix and United Airlines for Oct. 20. Meta and Tesla are expected Oct. 21. All dates are expected, not confirmed.

Source: Charles Schwab. schwab

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

SCIENCE & HEALTH ⚕️

U.S. measles cases pass 4,080, far above all of 2025
The CDC counted 4,080 confirmed cases as of Oct. 8, up 193 in a week. That compares with 2,289 for all of 2025. There have been 414 hospitalizations and two CDC-confirmed deaths. Pennsylvania separately reports five deaths tied to its outbreak, and the CDC recently changed how it sources death data, which has drawn scrutiny. New York declared a statewide disaster emergency over its outbreak. A newer CDC update was not located by the cutoff.

Source: Reuters (Oct. 9); Contagion Live. gvwire

Siberian plague-institute worker’s death remains unexplained

Russia’s health watchdog says a 28-year-old Irkutsk lab technician died of “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” and that extensive testing found no microorganisms tied to her work. A hospital was quarantined. Unconfirmed local media reports claim pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 contacts were placed under medical observation. The plague claim is unverified, and I found no later official update.

Source: AP (Oct. 5); Gulf News. wloxgulfnews

Forgotten museum fossil reveals new tiger-sized dinosaur

A skull fragment acquired by London’s Natural History Museum in 1924 belongs to a new species, Invictibellatrix amberina, the first known European megaraptoran, per a Royal Society Open Science study. It lived about 120 million years ago on the Isle of Wight. Its estimated 3–4 meter length is extrapolated from relatives, not measured.

Source: ScienceDaily; University College London. sciencedailyucl

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

NATIONAL SECURITY 🛡️

MI5 chief: Iran and Russia escalating hybrid campaigns; Iran now eyeing military sites

In his Oct. 13 annual speech, Ken McCallum said Iran-linked operations led to more than 50 arrests in Britain over the past year. He cited a shift toward “harder targets” such as military sites, and said Russia is escalating hybrid warfare against Ukraine’s allies. The suspected plot against RAF Fairford, a U.S.-used base, was described by Britain’s prime minister as “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. McCallum declined to comment because of the ongoing investigation.

Source: Reuters; AP; Boston Globe. al-monitorThe Boston Globe

Alleged Chinese agent held without bail in Taiwan-leader surveillance case

California realtor Wanying “Heather” Zhang was arrested at LAX Oct. 4 and charged with acting as an unregistered PRC agent. The FBI complaint alleges she surveilled the Seattle-area home of Taiwan’s president’s son. A magistrate ordered her detained as a flight risk. Her lawyers say the case rests on a single day of alleged surveillance, and she intends to prove her innocence. She is presumed innocent.

 Source: CBS News; Fox News; SCMP; Taiwan News. groundscmp

White-powder envelopes sent to election offices
Several election facilities received envelopes containing white powder this week. Authorities said no harmful substance was immediately identified in the latest incidents, and election-official groups condemned the threats. The specific offices and any suspect were not detailed in the reporting reviewed.

Source: Fox News. Fox News

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS 🪖

CRS: 81 U.S. aircraft lost or damaged in Iran war

An updated Congressional Research Service report counts 81 aircraft and drones lost or damaged since February, with equipment losses estimated at $1.9–3.3 billion. Crewed losses include 12 F-15Es, seven KC-135s, two A-10s, an F-35A and an E-3. CRS cautions that some damaged aircraft have returned to service and that figures may change.

Source: Gray/Military Times reporting on the CRS report. abcnews4

“Mother of all bombs” options prepared; no strike ordered

Sources told CBS that the White House and Pentagon have plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian military sites if ordered. The Pentagon says it plans for a range of scenarios, and the White House won’t discuss them. Trump said last week the U.S. would not attack before the midterms. Trump ruled out nuclear weapons but floated using a MOAB, and has said the U.S. “may have to” hit the Pickaxe Mountain site later.
This is contingency planning, not an operation.

Source: CBS News; CNN (as cited); Fox News. CBS NewsFox News

Trump announces Montana “super range” for advanced weapons testing

At a Wednesday rally in Kalispell, Trump said the Department of War will establish a new range to test autonomous weapons, space and electronic warfare, and supersonic and hypersonic systems. This is an announcement only, and I found no Pentagon timeline or site details.

Source: Fox News. Fox News

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

OTHER NOTABLE AND UNUSUAL STORIES 🌀

Houthi attacks upend Saudi sports calendar

Netflix’s Six Kings Slam was cancelled or postponed, and the WTA Finals were moved to the U.S. Al-Nassr matches and an Olympic BMX qualifier were also disrupted. Organizers insist the Asian Cup, Jan. 7–Feb. 5, remains on schedule, though South Korea’s players’ union has voiced safety concerns.

Source: AP/CBS News. CBS News

Musk’s America PAC confirms $276 million to GOP groups in three months

A representative for the PAC confirmed the figure to Fox News, including $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which backs Ken Paxton in Texas. This corroborates earlier New York Times reporting.

Source: Fox News; New York Times (as cited). Fox News

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

AMERICA FIRST READ 🇺🇸

Analysis, not news reporting.

Fuel costs are the thread running through today’s stories. Gasoline is near $4.33, headline CPI is 3.7%, Brent is near $110 and Hormuz attacks are at wartime highs, 17 days before the midterms. Fox’s poll found cost of living is voters’ top economic worry (60%), and 74% rate the economy negatively. The reported pause on Iran strikes until after Nov. 3 looks politically driven, but MOAB planning and Trump’s own comments suggest it is conditional. Whether Tehran de-escalates is the biggest unknown.

The diesel deal is a trade-off.

Supporters can argue any added supply helps at the pump. But analysts say the volumes barely move prices, while the cost is real: bipartisan criticism, strained ties with Kyiv, and an “energy ceasefire” Ukraine says Russia isn’t honoring. Until that compliance gap closes, the deal looks like more signal than supply.

On election security, the DOJ suit and the threats to election offices cut in different directions. The suit’s 20,000-plus count is an allegation awaiting a court. Threats against election workers are unacceptable regardless of party. Record early turnout in Georgia suggests voter confidence is holding.

In Bend, the confirmed facts are that an armed bystander and a tackling teacher stopped the attack, and that the shotgun was bought by the shooter’s mother. A gun-policy fight is under way, but motive and the full picture are still unestablished, and conclusions should wait on investigators.

Ahead: Israel’s election Oct. 27, the Fed on Oct. 28, Q3 GDP on Oct. 29 and USPS ballot measures from Oct. 24.

text:
John Allen Gaither: The Missing-Person Case That Uncovered a Hidden Room

In December 2023, 42-year-old John Allen Gaither was last known to be alive in Gulfport, Mississippi, where he lived with his mother, Jerri Roby. When his family could no longer reach him, they reported him missing, prompting an investigation.

Roby initially told police that John had taken an Uber to Louisiana to purchase a car. Investigators found no record supporting that account. She later offered other explanations, claiming he had travelled to meet a woman in the Philippines or gone to Mexico to help someone escape a drug cartel.

Meanwhile, messages that appeared to come from John continued reaching his relatives. Investigators alleged that Roby had forged a letter, sent messages using his phone, and persuaded her boyfriend to contact family members while pretending to be John. She also reportedly took the phone to Florida to make it appear that he was still travelling.

The investigation took a significant turn when police discovered that Roby had purchased materials including sand, straw, plastic sheeting, seal tape and a large bag from a hardware store before John was reported missing.

On January 18, 2024, investigators searched the home and discovered a concealed wooden box behind a false wall. John’s body was inside, covered with materials that reportedly matched the items purchased earlier. An autopsy determined that he had died from a gunshot wound to the back of the head.

After the discovery, Roby reportedly claimed that John had shot himself and somehow ended up inside the box. The discovery transformed a missing-person investigation into a criminal inquiry focused on the circumstances surrounding his death and the efforts to make his disappearance appear otherwise.

Disclaimer: This historical account is presented for educational purposes in a non-graphic manner.

text:
John Wrighten sued South Carolina in 1946 to enter a law school that would not have him, and the state built an entire separate one rather than let him through the door. Then he enrolled in that school, finished it, and had to pass a written bar exam that white graduates had been excused from since 1886.

The exemption vanished while he was still a student in the building his own lawsuit paid for. He got the door open and they took the handle off it.

In the spring of 1950, two men walked out of Orangeburg, South Carolina holding law degrees that were also law licenses. Their names were Albert A. Kennedy and Julius Thomas Williams Jr.

Neither man ever sat for a bar examination, because South Carolina did not require one of them. Under a rule the state had kept since 1886, a diploma from one of its law schools was itself admission to the bar.

That rule was sixty-four years old when Kennedy and Williams used it.

It did not survive the next twelve months.

By 1951 the diploma privilege was gone. Every law graduate in the state, white or Black, now had to pass a written examination graded by six practicing lawyers.

The privilege had been born in a room Black men were already put out of once.

South Carolina's public law school in Columbia was integrated during Reconstruction, and it was the only state university in the South that admitted and graduated Black students in those years. Between 1868 and 1876 it turned out thirty-nine lawyers, and eleven of them were Black.

The first was Walter Raleigh Jones.

On June 7, 1877, a joint resolution of the General Assembly closed the law school entirely. It reopened in 1884 for white students only, and two years after that its graduates were handed automatic admission to the bar.

The exemption arrived once there was nobody left in the building it could benefit but white men.

It stayed that way for two generations. Then a young man from Charleston started writing letters.

John Howard Wrighten came up through the Avery Normal Institute, the first accredited secondary school for Black children in Charleston. He graduated in 1943 and wrote to the College of Charleston that same year, asking what a Black applicant would have to do to be admitted.

Nothing came of it.

So in 1944 he went back to Avery and organized thirty-two seniors to do it with him. They wrote their letters as an assignment in Julia Brogdon's course, a class the school listed on its schedule as Problems in Democracy.

The College of Charleston was a municipal college then, funded by the city, which was the entire basis of the students' argument.

By that fall it was not a municipal college anymore. It had gone private, and the students were refused.

City officials offered Avery six scholarships to South Carolina State College in Orangeburg to settle the matter, which is the kind of offer that tells you the letters landed.

Wrighten served in World War II and came home the way a lot of Black veterans came home, done asking politely. On June 30, 1946, he applied to the University of South Carolina School of Law.

He was turned down on the ground of race and he sued, and the NAACP sent Thurgood Marshall to argue it. In the federal district court in Charleston, Judge J. Waties Waring held that a Black resident of the state was entitled to the same opportunity and facilities afforded to white residents for a legal education.

Waring then gave South Carolina three ways to comply.

Admit Wrighten to the law school in Columbia, or close that law school down. Or build a separate law school of substantially equal quality for Black students.

The state took the third door before the ink dried.

The General Assembly appropriated two hundred thousand dollars for a law school at South Carolina State College and thirty thousand more for its library. It opened on September 17, 1947, with nine students.

Marshall told his own client not to enroll in it. He called what the state had thrown together a Jim Crow dump in South Carolina, and he was not being unkind to the men who would teach there.

He was describing an appropriation.

In April 1950 the University of South Carolina dedicated a new home for its own law school in Columbia. That building cost two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.

The state had spent less on an entire law school for Black South Carolinians than on one building for white ones, and it had done both inside of thirty-six months.

Wrighten waited two years and enrolled at Orangeburg anyway, in September 1949. Kennedy and Williams got there ahead of him.

They finished in 1950, and because the rule still stood that spring, South Carolina handed two Black men licenses to practice law without asking either of them a single question. Then the rule was gone.

Matthew J. Perry Jr. graduated from the same school the very next year and had to sit the written examination.

He had grown up in Columbia and served in Europe as an Army sergeant. On a troop train layover in Alabama during the war he went looking for something to eat in a segregated depot.

He found Italian prisoners of war being served inside the whites-only dining room while Black American soldiers took their meals through a window.

Perry passed the bar on his first attempt. He opened an office in Spartanburg, the first Black lawyer that city had seen since the 1930s.

John Wrighten was admitted to the South Carolina bar in 1953, by examination.

The man whose lawsuit built the school did not get what the school's first graduates got. He sued a door open and the state pulled the handle off before he reached it.

A South Carolina legislator wrote to a colleague around that time that the new requirement would bar Negroes and some undesirable whites from practicing in the state. That letter was surfaced by William Hine, who taught history at South Carolina State for decades.

Hine was blunt when a reporter asked him about it in 2020, that examinations had always been a resource the white community controlled, and that the men who wrote them knew it.

Here is the part almost nobody knows.

The diploma privilege was not the only door South Carolina closed.

The state also allowed admission by reading law, the old apprenticeship route, studying in a practicing attorney's office instead of attending a school. That route was eliminated in 1957, shortly after a Black applicant used it.

South Carolina also allowed reciprocity, admitting lawyers already licensed in other states. That was abolished in January 1972, not long after a Black member of the Oklahoma bar applied under it.

Three routes into the profession, three closures, each one arriving right behind a Black man who had found the way through.

That is not a theory circulating on the internet. It is an argument four Black law graduates laid out in a federal courtroom, and it is printed in the reported decision.

Their names were David Richardson, Patrick Kelly, Hiram Spain, and Patricia King.

Richardson held a law degree from American University, Kelly and Spain from Howard, King from North Carolina Central. Every one of them had satisfied every requirement South Carolina set for admission to its bar except the examination.

They sued the Board of Law Examiners, and in 1976 the case reached the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit. They put the three dates on the table side by side and asked the court to look at them together.

The Examiners answered that the state had never written a rule explicitly barring Black lawyers, and that each change matched a national trend toward higher standards. They added that by the 1970 census South Carolina had the highest proportion of Black lawyers of any state in the country.

That proportion was three and four tenths percent.

The court ruled the evidence fell short of proving a deliberate state scheme. The pattern argument failed.

But the judges kept reading, and what they found in the grading was its own kind of testimony.

One examiner told the court his method was to take the strongest paper in the pile, work out how many points it needed to become an A, and add that same number to everyone else's score. Another explained that his own cutoff never moved, that the magic passing point is 70, and he ranged up or down from there.

Kelly's average came to 69.6 and he was failed. Spain's came to 70.5 and he was failed.

A man who averaged 69.3 was passed.

The court held the Examiners had acted arbitrarily as to Spain and Kelly, and ordered on remand that both be certified as having passed the South Carolina bar. It took two Howard-trained lawyers a federal appeal to be handed what Kennedy and Williams received in 1950 for walking across a stage.

The school in Orangeburg lasted nineteen years and graduated fifty-one people, fifty men and one woman. Its library grew from seventy-five hundred volumes to twenty-one thousand five hundred and thirty-seven.

Cassandra Maxwell, the first Black woman admitted to the South Carolina bar, taught there.

Between 1951 and 1968, twenty-nine of the fifty Black lawyers admitted to the South Carolina bar came out of that one small building.

They defended the Friendship Nine in Rock Hill. They desegregated Clemson, the University of South Carolina, and the Charleston County schools.

One graduate, Ruben Gray, described driving across the state to represent people arrested at demonstrations and getting not even gas for your car. Ernest A. Finney Jr., class of 1954, became chief justice of the South Carolina Supreme Court.

Matthew Perry became the first Black federal judge in the state. There is a federal courthouse in Columbia with his name on it now.

The law school graduated its last class on May 15, 1966, and closed.

John Wrighten practiced in Charleston for decades and later pastored African Methodist Episcopal churches in Connecticut. When he died in 1996 at seventy-five, a Charleston attorney named Russell Brown said that among Black lawyers in that state he was the granddaddy of us all.

South Carolina still has no diploma privilege.

In the summer of 2020, with a pandemic filling the hospitals, more than a hundred and fifty South Carolina law graduates petitioned their state Supreme Court to admit them without an in-person examination. The court said no and held the exam.

Almost none of the people who signed that petition knew why the privilege they were asking for did not exist.

It ended the year two Black men in Orangeburg used it, and the state has never been made to explain that. Not in a courtroom, not in a legislative session, not in one official word since.

Kennedy and Williams, then Wrighten, then Richardson and Kelly and Spain and King.

The dates are all on file, in the statute books and in the Fourth Circuit reports, and they line up the way they line up whether anyone opens them or not. Somebody ought to be reading them.

John Wrighten fought for a door that was never supposed to open for him, and the people who followed him used that opening to change the law. I share stories like his because history is built by people who challenge the limits placed in front of them.

https://t.co/Vm6JEQyFTo
Every coffee helps keep these lost histories alive

text:
Hey Seth Joyner, I've got a few things to say to you, and I'd love for you to respond.

First, Luke Fahey is 5'11", NOT 5'5". You're 6'2", Seth. THREE inches taller. You're hardly a giant yourself.

But here's what really bothers me.

I coached Luke beginning in the second grade. He's 19 years old, and I can tell you without hesitation that he's the finest young man I ever coached.

Not just because of his talent, but because of his HEART. His desire to learn, improve, please his coaches, support his teammates, and become the best he can possibly be.

Luke is everything you'd want in a teammate.

And watching you, a 61-year-old former NFL player, publicly ridicule a 19-year-old kid trying to live his dream makes me wonder what kind of teammate YOU were.

Frankly, based on this display, I wouldn't have wanted you in my locker room.

I used to admire you, Seth. I really did. But you've embarrassed yourself.

And I'll bet you're so lazy, or perhaps just a little slow, that you haven't watched five minutes of Luke's film or bothered to learn anything about him.

Let me educate you.

7,021 passing yards.
68 touchdown passes.
Only 9 interceptions.
Nearly 69% completions.

And here's the part you probably know absolutely nothing about.

Luke shared quarterback duties for much of his high school career. He could have transferred somewhere else to be the unquestioned starter, but he stayed loyal to his school, his coaches, and his teammates.

He essentially put up those numbers with about TWO FULL SEASONS' worth of playing time!

That's character, Seth. That's leadership. That's being a TEAMMATE.

Now imagine being 19 years old, getting your first opportunity at Ohio State, coming into a game with five minutes remaining against the defending national champions, riding a 22-game winning streak, IN THEIR OWN STADIUM.

And instead of encouraging the young man, a former NFL veteran decides to make fun of his height on social media.

Seriously, Seth? Is that the best you've got?

Do you enjoy putting down young athletes, or are you simply too lazy to learn anything about them before opening your mouth?

Here's something else you should understand.

I hope Julian Sayin gets healthy and returns. Tavien St. Clair is a tremendous young talent, and he deserves his opportunity, too.

But Luke and Tavien have a great relationship. They'll compete, they'll push each other, and if Tavien earns the job, Luke will be genuinely happy for him.

Because Luke understands something you apparently forgot somewhere along the way.

THE TEAM COMES FIRST.

And that's why I question what kind of teammate you were. Because the attitude you're displaying is the exact opposite of what I taught young men about sportsmanship, loyalty, and character.

You were a great football player, Seth. Nobody can take that away from you.

But being a great football player doesn't automatically make you a great man.

And right now, you're acting like a bully picking on a kid who's done absolutely nothing to deserve it.

I'd LOVE to debate you about Luke, football, leadership, and what makes a great teammate. Anytime, Seth. Publicly. Let's do it.

And I'll leave you with one final challenge.

IF LUKE FAHEY STARTS AGAINST USC, YOU TAKE USC.

I'LL TAKE OHIO STATE AND GIVE YOU 11 POINTS!

How's that for confidence in a young man?

So what do you say, Seth?

Are you willing to stand behind your words, or are you just another loudmouth who finds it easier to criticize young men than recognize their accomplishments?

I'm waiting for your response.

And Seth, one last thing.

You might have been a better football player than Luke will ever be. Time will tell.

But when it comes to HEART, CHARACTER, LOYALTY, and being a TEAMMATE?

I'll take Luke Fahey on my team EVERY SINGLE TIME.

Or YOU can reach out to Luke and apologize for being a TOOL and offer encouragement to a great young man.

text:
Our hearts are heavy over the tragic news from the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, where a vehicle drove through a youth soccer game, taking the lives of a child and an adult and injuring others. In moments of sudden loss and shock, we are reminded of the fragility of life and our deep need for the peace, comfort, and salvation that are found only in Jesus Christ (Psalm 46:1; John 16:33).

Let us pray together:

“Heavenly Father, God of all comfort and the Father of mercies, we come to You brokenhearted for the families and community in Wichita. Surround the grieving parents, children, and loved ones with Your nearness. Comfort those who mourn, heal the injured, and strengthen the first responders, medical teams, and authorities as they continue their work. Lord, give supernatural peace that passes understanding to all who are affected (Philippians 4:6–7).

Father, in this dark hour we also cry out for the salvation of every person touched by this tragedy and of all who hear this message. Draw hearts to Your Son, Jesus Christ, the only Savior. Open eyes to see that life is brief and that eternity is certain. In Jesus’ name, Amen.”

A Message of Salvation

Scripture declares that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and that the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; 6:23). Yet God demonstrates His own love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Jesus, the Son of God, lived a perfect life, died on the cross to pay the penalty for our sins, and rose again the third day, conquering death and offering eternal life to all who believe (I Corinthians 15:3–4; John 3:16).

Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). If you recognize your need for forgiveness and a right relationship with God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone as your Savior and Lord. Believe that He died for you and rose again. Confess Him with your mouth and believe in your heart, and you will be saved (Romans 10:9–10). He offers forgiveness, new life, and the sure hope of eternal life with Him.

May the God of all comfort and the Prince of Peace be near to every hurting heart in Wichita and beyond. In Jesus’ name.

text:
Wilbert McLure (pictured) suffers his first defeat, in his 15th pro fight, on October 18, 1963, to Luis Rodriguez.

The AP, which unofficially scored it 7-2-1 for Rodriguez, would write:

"The ever-exuberant Luis Rodriguez dropped and drubbed the previously undefeated Wilbert (Skeeter) McClure of Toledo in a television 10 rounder at MSG last night. Rodriguez forced a relentless pace and fired fierce barrages to the body. In the early moments of the 3rd round he floored the fighting school teacher with a solid right to the jaw. McClure staggered to his feet at four and was given the manadatory eight count by referee Teddy Martin. Although dazed, he instinctively backed away from the over-eager Rodriguez who couldn't land another decisive blow. A minute later McClure lashed out with counter-punches and they traded punches at a furious pace. Luis dominated the fight with his ceaseless attacks and fiery body punches."

Many critics of McLure's management team would protest that they were matching the 1960 Gold Medalist at Light Middleweight (in Rome) far too tough this early in his pro career. Rodriguez, 52-3-0 coming in, had lost two split decisions to the great Emile Griffith (one for the Welterweight Title and another a 10-round non-title bout, the other loss was another 10-round split decision to future titlist Curtis Cokes) and was far more seasoned and tested than McLure at this point.

"He beat me, no question about it. It's no shame losing to Luis Rodriguez." -Wilbert "Skeeter" McClure.

"He's a very good prospect. He has a very good left hand. I think he can become the middleweight champion unless I am the champion." -Luis Rodriguez.

From Mike Silver for Boxing Over Broadway (It is a long, but very  worthwhile, read):

Dr. Wilbert “Skeeter” McClure, the former professional boxer, passed away last week at the age of 81. Between 1958 and 1960, Skeeter McClure won virtually every important national and international amateur boxing championship including Amateur Athletic Union (AAU), Golden Gloves (Chicago and Inter-City), Diamond Belt, Tournament of Champions, and Pan American Games. The crowning achievement to his brilliant amateur career was winning the Olympic Gold Medal in the light-middleweight divisionat the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Italy.
McClure’s roommate at the Olympics was another Gold Medal winner named Cassius Marcellus Clay. At that point, McClure was considered to be a more accomplished boxer than Clay. But whereas Clay, later known as Muhammad Ali, won the professional heavyweight championship in 1964 and became the most recognized face on the planet, McClure’s once promising professional career stagnated, never living up to expectations. One wonders how things might have turned out had McClure, like Clay, been guided by the savvy Angelo Dundee instead of the incompetents with whom he entrusted his professional boxing career.
It is to McClure’s everlasting credit that he did not let the terrible mismanagement of his professional boxing career stop him from achieving great success in an entirely new profession. McClure had a college degree in literature and philosophy. After his pro career ended, he returned to school where he earned a master’s degree in counseling and, in 1973, a doctorate in psychology from Detroit’s Wayne State University. The Ohio native joined the teaching staff of Northeastern University in Boston, where he taught courses in counseling and psychology for five years. Over the next 20 years, McClure built a successful private clinical practice. In addition, he operated a consulting firm that provided corporations, non-profit foundations, and police departments with education and training in stress management, conflict resolution, team building, and performance evaluation.
Considering his post-boxing success, one might ask if it makes any difference that Skeeter did not win a professional boxing championship. I believe it absolutely does make a difference. McClure dedicated 17 years of his life to the sacrifice and discipline it takes to master the toughest of all sports. He had it within him not only to win a professional boxing title, but also to achieve all-time great status perhaps equal to or even exceeding that achieved by Muhammad Ali.
Bad decisions made by the people he trusted to guide him to a title destroyed those dreams. The history of his pro boxing career serves as a primer for how to ruin a brilliant young prospect through appallingly careless matchmaking.
As an Olympic gold medal winner, McClure would be a hot commodity if he were to turn pro today, especially considering that he was a college graduate. But the scenario in 1960 was quite different from today. An Olympic title, while desirable, did not automatically insure a megabuck promotional contract or a lucrative television deal.
After considering several management offers, McClure signed on with a wealthy Ohio businessman whose hobby was managing professional fighters. This person hired a trainer who had been affiliated with Archie Moore, the great light heavyweight champion. Regrettably for McClure, both the businessman and the trainer proved to be clueless in the ability to make appropriate matches for the young phenom.
McClure was drafted into the Army directly after the Olympics, but he was able to turn pro and fight several times while on leave. He won his ninth straight pro fight June 30, 1962 – a 6-round decision over Harold Richardson at Madison Square Garden. Teddy Brenner, the Garden’s matchmaker, was impressed with McClure’s performance and his sterling amateur background. Television was in need of new faces to fill a weekly schedule calling for almost fifty Garden main events per year. So, with a grand total of nine pro fights (5 KOs) and 39 rounds of professional experience, McClure was signed to fight the South American middleweight champion Farid Salim on August 4, 1962 at Madison Square Garden in front of a nationwide television audience. Salim, a rangy 6’ 2” middleweight had lost only two of forty professional fights.
McClure was excited to be headlining at the world famous arena and wanted to be ready for his first major test as a pro.  I asked my trainer: ‘Is he a boxer? Does he have fast hands? What’s he got?’ And the answer I received was: ‘I don’t know.’   What the [expletive]! My first TV fight…10 rounds…and the son-of-a-gun doesn’t know anything about my opponent! No one [today] would do that to a fighter with a Gold Medal.”  McClure shook his head in disgust.  It was the same thing with everyone else I fought. I’d ask: ‘What has he got?’  Every first round was a surprise.
Despite the lack of advance knowledge, the former Olympian, a 12-to-5 underdog, was more than up to the task. He won a unanimous decision. His superlative boxing skills were a revelation to many who witnessed the bout. One reporter wrote:  McClure moves with the grace of a young Ray Robinson, hits with authority, and fights back furiously when hurt. Comparing a boxer with only ten pro bouts to Robinson, the greatest fighter who ever lived, was a huge compliment. More experience before taking on top contenders was all that McClure would have needed in order to realize his full potential.
After four more fights, McClure was rated the eighth best middleweight in the world. But it was all happening too fast. There was little respite from one hard match to the next, all against top opposition. One didn’t have to be a boxing expert to know that McClure was being rushed into matches with fighters he should have avoided at that stage of his career.  At some point, the boxer must be tested against a quality opponent to see what he’s got, but the timing has to be right. Unfortunately, instead of being handled like a precious diamond in the rough that needed a master craftsman to cut and polish it, McClure was thrown to the lions while he was still learning the ropes as a pro.
Considering his spectacular amateur accomplishments and the tremendous promise shown in his early professional bouts, the ruination of that great potential, through no fault of his own, makes Wilbert Skeeter McClure the most poorly managed fighter in the history of the sport.
This is how it evolved: Six weeks after the bout with Farid Salim, McClure returned to his hometown of Toledo, Ohio and won a unanimous 10-round decision over tough Tony Montano, a 37-bout pro who’d competed with several world ranked boxers. Three weeks after the bout with Montano, McClure was back in the Garden meeting 63-bout veteran Gomeo Brennan. Once again displaying fighting spirit and superb boxing smarts, McClure won a hard-fought 10-round decision over a far more experienced opponent.  In early 1963, he returned to Toledo to outpoint former welterweight contender Ted Wright, a veteran of 60 professional bouts.
Amazingly, despite his limited professional experience, he was good enough to be competitive with these seasoned veterans, even outpointing them, but every fight was tough. He certainly wasn’t being overprotected, that’s for sure. In fact, in his 33 professional fights, only five opponents had losing records.  As if to emphasize this point, in his next fight, on October 18, 1963, McClure was matched against the great former welterweight champion Luis Rodriguez in yet another nationally televised fight from Madison Square Garden.
Rodriguez was a substitute for Jose Gonzales, a granite-chinned contender who six months earlier had withstood the bombs of “Hurricane” Carter and stopped the feared puncher on a cut in the sixth round. When Gonzales was injured in training, he pulled out of the scheduled bout with McClure; Luis replaced him. A bout with Gonzales would have meant another punishing contest for McClure, but taking on Rodriguez made even less sense.
McClure didn’t have to ask about Rodriguez. The great Cuban boxer was a former welterweight champion and one of the ten best fighters in the world. His only losses in 55 bouts were against Emile Griffith and Curtis Cokes. Rodriguez was capable of beating the world’s top welterweights and middleweights. He had scored a stunning ninth-round knockout of middleweight contender Denny Moyer in his most recent fight. Luis had a total of 430 professional rounds compared to McClure’s mere 14 fights and 85 rounds.
McClure knew that he was not ready for Rodriguez. He told his manager and trainer that he thought they were crazy for accepting him as an opponent at this stage of his career.  We argued for two days, said McClure. I was just so tired of all this crap. Isolated in a remote New Jersey training camp, the young fighter was fatigued and disgusted. But, his handlers eventually convinced him to accept the match, saying that his weight advantage of nine pounds would give him an edge.
Meeting a fighter of Rodriguez’s stature in his 15th professional bout was both negligent and stupid. Compare it to the early career of future middleweight champion Marvin Hagler who turned pro after winning the National AAU light-middleweight championship in 1973. In Hagler’s 15th pro bout, he won a 10-round decision over Sugar Ray Seales, the 1968 Olympic gold medalist. It was Seale’s first defeat in 22 bouts.
Hagler’s next two opponents had a combined record of 5-14-3.  Another future middleweight champion, Roy Jones Jr., a light middleweight Silver medalist in the 1988 Olympics, had a spectacular amateur record similar to McClure’s.  In his 15th pro bout, Jones KO’d Lester Yarbrough who came into the ring with a 12-16-1 record and would win only one of his next 34 bouts. Neither of these future pro champions faced the type of brutal competition that McClure had to contend with during his first two years as a pro.
Of course it was a forgone conclusion that Skeeter would lose. Once again displaying the heart and talent of a true champion, and despite being dropped for the first time, the overmatched Olympian actually gave Rodriguez a tough fight. The Cuban won a unanimous 10-round decision, but he had to work hard for the victory. Even Rodriguez was impressed. Give that kid another year, he said, and he’ll be champion.
After that fight, Skeeter should have taken a rest and then taken on a series of lesser opponents, while at the same time perfecting his professional skills.
Instead, Brenner insisted on a rematch two months later. After all, their first televised fight was exciting and interesting so why not do it again? McClure’s management should have refused the rematch.  It is a truism in the unforgiving world of professional boxing that a quick rematch between an inexperienced boxer and an old pro is just asking for trouble. The old pro will use his vast experience to figure out what to do in the rematch while the inexperienced boxer will be at a distinct disadvantage. And that is exactly what happened. Rodriguez adjusted his strategy and concentrated his attack on McClure’s body to slow him up and bring down his guard.  In Round 6, Rodriguez dropped McClure for an 8-count with a solid left hook to the jaw. Once again McClure got up and fought his heart out. He was able to win a few rounds but lost another unanimous decision in a punishing fight. Putting McClure into the ring with Luis Rodriguez for his 15th and 16 fight was not just bad matchmaking, it bordered on criminal negligence.
A young boxer doesn’t walk away from a series of tough and punishing fights without paying a price. If it happens often enough there will come a time in the abused boxer’s professional life when something changes within him.  It can happen after one vicious beating, or it can take place over the course of several tough fights with too little time to rest between them. The change can be dramatic, or it can be subtle and unrecognizable except to an experienced trainer or someone close to the boxer. The damage is both physical and psychological. Eventually the law of diminishing returns takes effect as progress ends and potential is blunted.
The boxing portion of this story could very well end here even though Skeeter went on to fight 14 more times over the next four years. Five months after the Rodriguez debacle, there was a 10-round decision loss to future light-heavyweight champion Jose Torres (another Garden fight McClure needed like a hole in the head); only two fights in 1965, and in 1966, a pair of back-to-back 10-rounders spaced two months apart with murderous-hitting middleweight contender Rubin “Hurricane” Carter. McClure lost a decision in the first bout and fought to a draw in the second. The cost of those two fights added to the erosion of this once brilliant prospect. The decline was underscored four months later when he lost a 10-round decision to unrated Harold Richardson, the same fighter he previously had beaten easily. It was McClure’s 24th professional fight and his fifth loss. Comparisons to Sugar Ray Robinson were long past. He had been put in too deep too early, and sunk.
Yet, it took a while for this proud and intelligent boxer to finally accept the inevitable, to acknowledge that the boxing part of his life was ended. In 1967, after being stopped for the first time in his career by Johnny Smith and then losing a lackluster 10-round decision to England’s Johnny Pritchett, McClure hung up his gloves. His record was 23-7-1 (11 KOs). Three years later, feeling the itch to give it one more try, he had two more fights and then retired for good.
Although a large part of the blame for McClure’s failed boxing career goes to his managers, the person who was most responsible for ruining him was Teddy Brenner, the powerful Madison Square Garden matchmaker. Both Brenner and Harry Markson, the director of the Garden’s boxing department, were uninterested (or perhaps incapable) of using the resources, reputation, and influence of the world’s most famous arena to its fullest capacity. Developing and nurturing new talent was not a priority with them. There are people who mistakenly hail Brenner as a great matchmaker. The facts do not support that opinion. During his tenure at the Garden (1959 to 1977), Brenner made some good matches, but he did far more damage by destroying the careers of at least a score of very promising young fighters, including McClure, by overmatching them against superior opposition before they were ready. This pattern was repeated far too often. Brenner knew better but just didn’t care.  If the result of a match ended up ruining a prospect, so be it. It was of no concern to either Brenner or Markson. Their weekly paychecks arrived whether they put on a good show or not. They would also abuse their power by favoring certain “house fighters” handled by compliant managers who never argued with Brenner’s choice of opponent. Making matters worse, the marketing skills of Brenner and Markson were negligible. The great arena was running on its reputation and interest was dwindling. One time, near the end of their tenure, in a fit of pique they revoked the press privileges of a journalist who dared to criticize one of their awful matches in print. So much for freedom of the press.
In those days the prestige of appearing in a main event at Madison Square Garden was second only to winning a world title. Even when matched against an opponent that was all wrong for their fighter, managers were reluctant to turn down a Garden main event.  But it didn’t have to be that way. In Los Angeles, during the same period, promoters George Parnassus and Eileen Eaton were carefully developing and nurturing local talent and making the sport hugely popular without benefit of a national television sponsorship. But because this is an article in tribute to Wilbert McClure, I won’t go into further details about the destructive nature of Brenner and Markson’s arrogance and incompetence. Suffice it to say that boxing suffered as a result.
McClure was not prone to self-pity, nor did he live in the past. His positive attitude helped him to start over in an entirely new field. But boxing was not totally out of his life. From 1995 to 1998, he served as chairman of the Massachusetts Boxing Commission where one of his chief priorities was the athletes’ safety. He especially was concerned about over-the hill-boxers who can no longer properly defend themselves yet still are allowed to fight. The boxing community, said McClure, especially the state commissions, ought to have more courage lifting the licenses of fighters who cannot and should not do it anymore. During my tenure as chairman, I was threatened with lawsuits by managers because we suspended those boxers who couldn’t fight anymore.
When asked to evaluate today’s fighters McClure’s response was precise. You cannot become skilled and polished if you are fighting two or three times a year. When you’ve got fighters challenging for a world title with 15 pro fights, you know you’ve got a problem. It makes it difficult to appraise the top boxers of today based on what they have accomplished. It is not scientifically sound, accurate, or fair. I feel sorry for Roy Jones Jr. because he hasn’t fought a great or even a very skillful opponent yet. So he cannot be placed in the pantheon of great middleweights because it takes great opponents to make great fighters.
McClure also said that welterweight champ Oscar de La Hoya, although still a work in progress, was lucky that there were no Kid Gavilans around to test him.  Put Oscar in the ring with Gavilan when he was champion, or a Ray Robinson when he was champ or a Tony Zale. Those guys were tough, man. There isn’t any way in the damn world you’re going to hurt them…and they will hurt you badly. It is a lesson that Skeeter learned the hard way.
Wilbert “Skeeter” McClure, a gracious and intelligent man, made his mark both inside and outside of the boxing ring. But most importantly, he lived his life with meaning and purpose.

text:
Blocking Data Centers Is Gambling With America’s AI Future

Most people miss this: the AI race isn’t only about algorithms. It’s about compute. And compute lives in data centers. The best chip in the world is useless without power, cooling, and a building to put it in.

1. The brakes are on

This year, Democrats at multiple levels have moved to slow data center construction.

At the state level, Democratic lawmakers in New York advanced a one-year pause on permits for new data centers drawing 20MW or more, citing voter concerns over rising utility bills.

At the federal level, Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ), the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said he supports pausing AI data center construction. The industry’s trade group pushed back hard, warning that a halt would ration access to cloud services and weaken US competitiveness.

And it’s worth noting who else opposed New York’s ban: not just Republicans, but unions and economic development groups. Data centers mean construction jobs, electrician jobs, and local tax revenue. This isn’t a simple “Big Tech vs. regular people” story.

2. Why this is a mistake

The AI race is an infrastructure race between nations. China is building power plants and compute capacity at a speed everyone can see. The US leads in chips and models, but compute has to physically land somewhere. That takes land, power, and fast permitting.

Pause for a year, and capital won’t wait. It moves to other states and other countries. A year in AI can be an entire model generation. Trading leadership in a defining technology for short-term utility bill concerns is a bad deal.

The better answer: speed up grid buildout, require data centers to bring their own power or pay their fair share of grid costs, and set clear community benefit standards. Not a blanket ban.

3. The investment case: one of the strongest assets in CRE

I’m an accountant. I look at the numbers.

Returns: Data center REITs posted an average 18.7% total return year-to-date through late June, beating broader CRE indices and the tech sector.
Valuations: Cap rates on stabilized, hyperscaler-anchored assets have compressed to 4.2%. Lower cap rates mean buyers are paying up.
Financing: Private equity committed $47.2 billion to digital infrastructure in H1 2026. Tenants are Amazon, Microsoft, and Google on long-term leases, exactly what lenders love.
Demand: Utilization across 50 major global markets is 94.6%, with average vacancy at just 5.4%. Compare that to office.
Runway: JLL projects roughly 100GW of new capacity from 2026 to 2030, creating over $1 trillion in real estate value.

4. Bottom line

When an industry offers some of the best returns, the easiest financing, the strongest demand, and matters for national competitiveness, policy should help it solve its power and community problems, not hit pause. Blocking data centers doesn’t just hurt investors. It weakens America’s position in the AI era.

The other side (worth knowing)

Utility bills are a real issue. Data centers use enormous amounts of power, and grid upgrade costs can get passed on to households. Supporters of a pause argue they’re protecting residents by settling “who pays” first, not opposing AI.
It’s not only Democrats. Some New York Republicans backed the pause, and Marietta, Georgia froze all data center applications for six months after resident pushback. Local resistance is largely bipartisan.
“Highest returns” isn’t settled. Green Street data shows data center values rose only about 1% in Q1 2026, while strip centers and senior housing led. Some analysts warn of overbuilding, and a 4.2% cap rate already prices in near-perfect execution.
“Losing the AI race” is a projection, not a fact. The bigger US bottleneck may be grid and transmission capacity, not permits. How much a one-state pause affects national capacity is still debated.

Opinion only, not investment advice.

text:
Most people are shocked when they learn how many free Black Americans actively helped found the United States—not as bystanders, but as soldiers, petitioners, property owners, and patriots who risked everything for the same liberty the Founders proclaimed.

Constitutional educator KrisAnne Hall has long taught this overlooked history (drawing from primary sources and classic works like William Cooper Nell’s The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution). By the time of the Revolution, there were already tens of thousands of free Black people in the colonies—roughly 5–10% of the total Black population. Many lived, worked, owned property, ran businesses, and participated in civic life, especially in the North.

Thousands more free Black men (plus enslaved men who earned their freedom through service) fought for American independence in integrated units. Estimates put the number of Black Patriots at 5,000–9,000 soldiers and sailors across the war. They weren’t exceptions; they were part of the force that won independence.

Some of the names Hall highlights:
•Crispus Attucks, a free man (formerly enslaved), was the first to die in the Boston Massacre—the Revolution’s first martyr. His funeral was one of the largest Boston had ever seen.
•Peter Salem, a free Black soldier, is credited with killing British Major Pitcairn at Bunker Hill, helping turn the battle. Washington himself praised his courage.
•Ned Hector, who refused orders to retreat at Brandywine and Germantown, saved his wagon and horses, and was later honored.
•George Middleton, a free Black colonel in a Massachusetts militia unit (connected to the “Bucks of America”), later founded the African Benevolent Society to support widows and orphans of Black Revolutionary soldiers.
•James Forten, born free in Philadelphia, served in the Navy as a teenager, refused a British offer of comfort in exchange for switching sides, and spent months in a prison ship rather than betray the American cause. He later became a successful sailmaker and early abolitionist leader.
•Prince Hall and others used the language of the Declaration of Independence itself in petitions demanding liberty and equality.

These men (and others like James Armistead Lafayette, who spied for the Americans at Yorktown) weren’t fighting for abstract ideals—they were fighting for the same natural rights the Founders said belonged to all men. 

Several states even offered permanent freedom to enslaved men who enlisted. Free Black freemen in multiple states met property qualifications, voted locally, and helped ratify the Constitution.

This history doesn’t erase the real evil of slavery or the contradictions of the era. It simply restores the full picture: free Black Americans were present, armed, and invested in the founding of the country from the beginning. Hall argues that erasing or minimizing their contributions leaves everyone—especially Black Americans—robbed of a fuller, more accurate story of American liberty.

If this surprises you, dig into the records and Hall’s teaching on the “forgotten framers.” The truth is more interesting (and more unifying) than the simplified version most of us were taught.
