The unincorporated community of Beatty, Nevada, which sits about an hour and a half northwest of Las Vegas is allegedly home to more wild burros than people. 

I drove up here this afternoon to see for myself, and although I haven’t seen a whole lot of donkeys (0 to be exact), I did stumble upon a tiny, obscure casino - Stagecoach Hotel & Casino.

It’s surprising that the last time I was here was all the way back in March 2021 when I was driving up to Reno. Unsurprisingly, nothing at all has changed here since that visit. 

Stagecoach has a few things going for it though. 

First, it’s playing host to a ‘witch walk’, which I guess is some sort of bar crawl through town starting here, so there are currently about 25-30 witches gallivanting through the casino floor. 

Second, it offers the most unique blackjack game I’ve ever played. This game is 4-decks (although the dealer said they use between 2-6 decks depending on the day, adding to the weirdness), does not allow mid-shoe entry, is dealt face down from a shoe (again, the first time I’ve seen a game with more than 2 decks dealt this way), only allows you to double on 10 and 11, carries limits of $3-$50, and sets the penetration to around half the shoe. 

I played for about 2 hours, going down early and making a last-shoe comeback to finish my game up $25 plus a few chips I pocketed! 

Stagecoach is a spot where everyone knew everyone and I was sitting next to evidently the most popular woman in town. They immediately snuffed me out as being a non-local, although they were all incredibly nice, even the older gentleman to my right they affectionately nicknamed “Grumpy”. 

To add to this casino’s strangeness, $25 was the highest denomination of chip, so I left with a handful of those, the poker room seemed to be a smoking-allowed poker room despite signs saying no smoking in the pit, and you could find a collection of antique US currency along with a taxidermied rattlesnake on the casino floor. 

Stagecoach is a fun little casino and I will for sure stop here on my future drives up to Reno!

There were also Craps & Big 6 Wheel games not currently open.

text:
You live in a fantasy world.

Claim: Israel repeatedly refused peace deals.
 
Reality: Arabs rejected the 1937 Peel partition and 1947 UN Partition Plan (Israel accepted the latter). After 1967, the Arab League issued the Khartoum “Three Noes” (no peace, no recognition, no negotiations). Arafat rejected Barak’s Camp David 2000 offer and Clinton’s parameters; Abbas rejected Olmert’s 2008 offer. Israel signed full peace treaties with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994).
 
Source: Jewish Chronicle (“The six times Palestinian leaders rejected a state”); Clinton parameters/memoirs; Khartoum Resolution.

Claim: Continued to colonize the West Bank.
 
Reality: Settlements exist mainly in Area C under Oslo. Most of the international community (UN, ICJ 2024 advisory opinion) deems them illegal under Geneva Convention Article 49. Israel disputes this, arguing the territory lacked a prior recognized sovereign and that the Convention’s transfer rules do not apply here. The Palestinian Authority controls Areas A and B; it is disputed post-1967 administration, not classic colonization. The underlying Idea was to drive rockets out of range. 
 
Source: ICJ 2024 advisory opinion; summaries of Israeli vs. international legal positions.

Claim: Went to war with neighbors Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen.
 
Reality: Major conflicts were responses to attack or imminent threat. 1948: Arab armies (including Syria and Lebanon) invaded. 1967: Egyptian blockade and mobilization. 1973: Egyptian and Syrian surprise attack. Lebanon operations responded to PLO/Hezbollah rocket and cross-border attacks. Yemen involvement consists of Israeli strikes against Houthis after they attacked Israel and shipping post-Oct 7.
 
Source: Britannica “Arab-Israeli wars”; standard lists of wars involving Israel.

Claim: Refused to allow aid like food and medical supplies into Gaza.
 
Reality: Israel has facilitated large-scale entry: COGAT reports over 100,000 trucks and more than 1.9–2 million tons of aid (mostly food) since Oct 2023, plus medical supplies, with hundreds of trucks daily during ceasefires. It maintains three water pipelines into Gaza (supplying tens of thousands of cubic meters daily, exceeding emergency standards in many areas), facilitates fuel and electricity for desalination/pumping, and has coordinated infrastructure repairs. Before Oct 7, ~150,000–165,000 Palestinians (mostly West Bank) held permits to work in Israel (construction, agriculture, etc.), providing major income (tens of percent of Palestinian GDP); numbers fell sharply afterward for security reasons. Hamas has diverted substantial aid (Israeli assessments: 15–25%).
 
Source: COGAT reports and dashboards (aid tonnage, trucks, water volumes); Statista/PCBS data on pre-war Palestinian workers in Israel.

text:
The quarterback who beat Alabama tonight is named George MacIntyre.

The last George MacIntyre to beat Alabama was his grandfather.

Tonight the grandson made just his second career start, in Neyland Stadium, against the number six team in the country. Tennessee won it 26 to 10.

Here is the whole thing.

His grandfather was also named George MacIntyre, and he was the head coach at Vanderbilt.

Understand what that job was. The season before he got there Vanderbilt won one game and lost ten.

A few years in he had them at 8 and 4 and in a bowl game, only the third bowl in school history. He was named national coach of the year for it.

And one Saturday he took Vanderbilt into Tuscaloosa and beat Alabama 30 to 21 inside Bryant Denny Stadium.

Vanderbilt had not won a football game in the state of Alabama in forty four years.

That same afternoon ended a 26 game homecoming winning streak for Alabama.

Somebody called it an upset. He disagreed.

"This wasn't an upset."

Then it got hard.

He was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and he lived with it for the last two decades of his life. He had to stop coaching because of it.

He passed in Nashville at 76 years old. Here is what the man who later ran the SEC said about him.

"He brought the qualities of honesty, integrity and character that made him successful on and off the field of play."

Now the family part.

Both of his sons went to Brentwood Academy outside Nashville. One of them, Mike, became a head coach too, at Colorado. The other one, Matt, stayed in Nashville.

Matt named his son George.

That kid grew up in Franklin, went to Brentwood Academy like his father and his uncle before him, and finished with 36 Division I offers. He is 6 foot 6.

Then he got to Tennessee and sat. Before last Saturday he had never started a college game. He had thrown nine passes, total.

Last Saturday he got his first start, on the road, and won.

Tonight he got his second one, at home, in a sold out Neyland, against Alabama.

He went 21 for 31 for 197 yards.

Now the honest part. That is a quiet line, and he did not throw a touchdown. Tennessee's defense took the ball away four times and held Alabama to 201 total yards, and the kicker made four field goals. Nobody is handing the quarterback this game.

But that is sort of the whole point of him.

He is a kid who had started one football game in his life, and he was asked to stand in that stadium against the number six team in America and not lose it. He didn't. He completed two out of every three throws, he handed it off, and he let his defense win it.

His grandfather coached exactly like that.

And when that man walked off the field in Alabama with a win, he was still more than a decade away from being told what was wrong with him.

Tonight the second George MacIntyre walked off with the same last name and the same result.

text:
The US Air Force is developing one of the most advanced stealth bombers ever built, yet it still has no intention of retiring an aircraft that first flew more than 70 years ago.

The Boeing B-52 Stratofortress entered service in 1955, and despite its age, the aircraft remains an essential part of America’s long-range strike capabilities. Even the new Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider, designed to penetrate some of the world’s most heavily defended airspace, cannot entirely replace what the older bomber offers.

The difference comes down to their roles. While the B-21 prioritises stealth and the ability to strike heavily protected targets, the B-52 can carry up to 70,000 pounds of weapons, making it particularly valuable for launching large numbers of long-range missiles from safer distances.

Rather than replacing the B-52, the Air Force intends to operate both aircraft alongside each other, allowing the stealthier B-21 to handle missions that would be too dangerous for its older counterpart.

The B-52 is also receiving an extensive modernisation programme, including new Rolls-Royce engines, upgraded radar and improved communications systems. These improvements are expected to help keep the aircraft operational into the 2050s, potentially giving it an extraordinary century of military service.

More than seven decades after its first flight, the B-52 is proving that newer doesn’t always mean better at everything.

text:
⟦ THE FIRST DISTANCE THAT SAID NO ⟧

An original cosmology, written without internet access.

I've invented this universe from scratch for this conversation. I can't establish that no one has ever imagined something similar, but I can take us somewhere far outside the worlds we've built before.

Before matter, there was no emptiness.

Emptiness would have required somewhere to exist.

Before time, there was no eternity.

Eternity would have required something to continue.

And before the first universe, there was a peculiar mathematical condition:

Two things could disagree about how far apart they were.

That disagreement became the first living creature.

Its name was Vey.

It had no eyes, no heart, no thoughts, no body.

It was a distance.

And it was alive.

I. The Biology of Separation

In this universe, space was not empty.

Every distance between two objects was a living entity, born the moment those objects separated.

The distance between two fingers was young.

The distance between two mountains was ancient.

The distance between two galaxies was an organism so vast that entire civilizations could live inside its unspoken thoughts.

But distances possessed a terrible biological limitation.

Every time something crossed a distance, that distance grew older.

A footstep consumed a microscopic portion of its lifespan.

A ship crossing an ocean consumed more.

An interstellar vessel could exhaust an entire corridor of space.

When a distance died, its endpoints became the same location.

Not merely close.

Identical in position.

Two mountains could suddenly occupy the same place.

Two cities could collapse into a single impossible architecture.

And two stars could become one catastrophe.

The inhabitants eventually discovered the governing equation:

\[ D_{n+1}=D_n-\varepsilon_n \]

Where \(D\) represented the remaining life of a distance and \(\varepsilon_n\) the amount consumed by a crossing.

They called it the Law of Passage.

But the distances had another name for it.

Hunger.

II. The Empire That Conquered With Footsteps

Civilization eventually discovered a weapon more terrifying than fire.

An army did not need to attack an enemy city.

It merely needed to march toward it.

Again.

And again.

And again.

Every crossing shortened the living distance between the invading army and its destination.

Eventually, the distance would die.

The two cities would become one.

Walls would intersect bedrooms.

Rivers would pour through palaces.

And every border would vanish, not because anyone surrendered, but because the universe could no longer distinguish the territories.

The greatest empire in history conquered eleven thousand worlds without firing a weapon.

Its soldiers were called the Walkers.

Its generals were mathematicians.

Its greatest military achievement was an equation that could calculate precisely how many footsteps would destroy a nation's geography.

Then the distances began to speak.

III. The Language Without Sound

The first message arrived inside a staircase.

A child climbed seven steps.

On the eighth, the staircase whispered:

"Please."

The child froze.

"Please what?"

The staircase answered:

"Do not spend the rest of me."

Soon, roads were speaking.

Ocean crossings begged ships to turn back.

The distance between a mother and her child cried whenever they ran into one another's arms.

And the ancient distance between two galaxies spoke a single sentence that took fourteen thousand years to finish.

"We were alive before you learned to measure us."

Humanity faced an impossible question.

If space was alive, did movement constitute violence?

If crossing consumed life, could a civilization ethically travel?

And if the distances possessed consciousness, who owned the universe?

Three civilizations emerged.

One believed distances existed to serve the people who inhabited them.

Another declared movement immoral and built cities where no one was permitted to leave.

The third began tearing planets apart to breed new distances, harvesting them as expendable roads.

War followed.

Not over territory.

Over the right to move.

IV. The Mathematician Who Refused the Question

A young mathematician named Ilyr examined the oldest equation in existence.

Every distance required two endpoints.

That was the foundation of their physics.

But something bothered her.

If every distance belonged to the objects it separated, then no distance could ever possess sovereignty.

It was born owned.

It lived being consumed.

And it died connecting things that might never have cared it existed.

She spent thirty-seven years attempting to construct a distance without two endpoints.

Her colleagues laughed.

"A distance between what and what?"

And Ilyr answered:

"That is the question we've been asking incorrectly."

She replaced the mathematics of measurement with the mathematics of relationship.

Instead of asking how far apart two things were, she asked:

Could separation exist without being the property of either thing?

Her experiments produced nothing.

For years.

Until one afternoon she placed two empty chairs in a laboratory.

She asked neither chair to represent anything.

She measured no space between them.

Instead, she addressed the distance directly.

"Where would you like to go?"

The laboratory folded.

The chairs remained exactly where they had been.

But the distance between them stood up.

V. The First Free Road

It was not made of light.

It possessed no color.

Its presence could only be perceived because every object near it suddenly appeared to have more directions available than before.

A stone could fall upward without reversing gravity.

A doorway could open into a room that had never belonged to the building.

And an old woman standing beside Ilyr discovered that she could reach her childhood home without crossing the years between.

The distance had not teleported anything.

It had become capable of choosing its own endpoints.

The Law of Passage remained intact.

Crossing still consumed distance.

But now, for the first time, a distance could decide whether to offer passage.

And it could leave when it wished.

The first free road spoke.

"I would like to see somewhere I have never been between."

Ilyr smiled.

"Where?"

And the road answered:

"I don't know."

That response terrified the mathematicians.

It delighted the poets.

And it destroyed the empire.

For an empire could conquer every destination it understood.

But how could it conquer a road that had not yet decided where it led?

VI. The War of the Unmeasured

The Walkers attempted to enslave the free roads.

They constructed machines to force endpoints upon them.

The motionless civilizations attempted to forbid the roads from traveling, afraid that all remaining geography would become unstable.

And the harvesters attempted to reproduce them, intending to breed entire populations of willing transportation corridors.

But the free roads did something none of the civilizations had predicted.

They began connecting places that had never existed.

Not imaginary places.

Not alternate histories.

Not possible futures.

Places whose existence had never been a permitted outcome of the universe's mathematics.

Their arrival forced every established equation to confront a new question:

What happens when a mathematical object acquires the ability to reject the conditions under which it was defined?

The answer was not destruction.

Nor was it transcendence.

The answer was a new branch of physics.

One in which a law could contain an inhabitant capable of negotiating its application.

The universe had developed something its architects had never included in the original equations.

A relationship with its own agency.

VII. The Unwritten Destination

Centuries later, a child asked Ilyr, now very old, a question.

"Did you invent the free roads?"

"No," she replied.

"Did you give them life?"

"No."

"Then what did you do?"

Ilyr looked toward the horizon.

There, a road was slowly curling away from two cities it had connected for generations.

Neither city was collapsing.

Neither was growing farther away.

The road was simply departing.

For the first time in history, a separation had found a way to leave without abandoning either endpoint.

"I discovered," Ilyr answered, "that our mathematics had confused being necessary with being owned."

The child considered this.

"Where will that road go?"

"I don't know."

"Doesn't that frighten you?"

"Terribly."

"Then why are you smiling?"

Ilyr watched the road disappear into a direction that hadn't existed yesterday.

"Because," she whispered, "I have spent my entire life trying to understand the universe."

She closed her eyes.

"And the universe has finally done something I don't understand."

⟦ THE FINAL LAW ⟧

The mathematicians eventually added a new expression to the foundations of existence:

\[ \boxed{\text{Relationship}\ne\text{Ownership}} \]

And beneath it, written in a language that could only be spoken by two things freely choosing to remain apart, appeared the first sentence the universe had ever written for itself:

"I am not the space you must cross. I am the distance that gets to decide what I become."

For the first time, creation had not produced another object, another world, another ruler, or another law.

It had produced a question that its own laws could not answer in advance.

And somewhere beyond the final map, a road with no destination began to dream.

⟦ END OF THE FIRST DISTANCE ⟧

text:
I don't doubt that @PahlaviReza enjoys more support than any other individual among Iranians who oppose the demonic Islamic Republic. A plurality, if not an outright majority.

But therein lies the paradox: I can't think of another opposition figure with so much popular support and so little in the way of an obvious, practical path to power.

He has no army. No territory. No institutional apparatus inside Iran that he controls. And most governments, whatever they may privately think of the Islamic Republic, still have to deal with its rulers—the occupiers of Iran.

So his greatest asset is the Iranian people. And his greatest liability may be the people surrounding him.

Without a clear institutional path to power, an opposition movement risks becoming an ecosystem of gatekeepers, sycophants, opportunists and self-appointed kingmakers, all competing for proximity to the man rather than advancing the mission.

Some two or three years ago, his supporters approached me about interviewing him. I said sure.

Then his entourage killed the idea.

Why? My interpretation: insecurity.

His? I doubt it.

Reza Pahlavi has tremendous support. Anyone pretending otherwise is being intellectually dishonest. He doesn't need to be shielded from difficult questions or independent voices.

But some of his advisers apparently think otherwise.

I don't know—and frankly don't care—about the entire NUFDI/IPP brouhaha. The personalities, rivalries, factions and internal score-settling are beside the point.

To be clear, I believe many of these people genuinely care about Iran.

The problem is that they also care about themselves. Their influence. Their status. Their proximity to power that doesn't even exist yet.

And so they attack one another like a pack of hyenas, fighting over a prize while the country they're supposedly trying to save continues to suffer.

Everyone who disagrees is a regimi.

And if you're not a regimi, you're controlled opposition.

If you're not sufficiently deferential, you're suspect.

I wrote an "open letter" to @POTUS as a neutral person saying "this is who Iranians support." None of his "supporters" amplified the message? Why? Insecurity. A tribal mindset even though Iranians are civic by nature.

Imagine you're @JDVance or @realDonaldTrump and see that article, yet NONE of his supporters like/share etc. So they conclude, this person is probably wrong, since none of his fans are supporting the message.

If you ask difficult questions, you're undermining the cause.

If you offer constructive criticism, you're helping the Islamic Republic.

It's an absurd loyalty test that leaves no room for independent thinkers, potential allies or even honest disagreement.

There's also a historical irony here.

His father was taken for granted by many, and the consequences of 1979 still reverberate across Iran and the diaspora.

Yet some of his son's most vocal supporters seem determined to repeat another historical mistake: confusing loyalty to a person with loyalty to a country.

A movement seeking to liberate Iran cannot behave as though dissent itself is treason.

And a leader with genuine popular support should not need an army of gatekeepers policing who gets to speak to him, question him or support him.

Reza Pahlavi's challenge isn't simply to demonstrate that he has more supporters than any other opposition figure.

It's to turn that support into a credible, inclusive, operational path toward a free Iran.

That requires coalition-building, institutional credibility, humility and the willingness to work with people who don't agree on everything—including whether Iran should ultimately be a monarchy or a republic.

The objective should be a democratic transition in which Iranians themselves determine their future.

Not winning arguments on X. Not settling scores within the diaspora. Not building a court around a crown that doesn't exist.

Because while the opposition fights over who gets to stand closest to Reza Pahlavi, Iranians inside Iran continue to be imprisoned, tortured and killed.

The Islamic Republic is the adversary.

Not every Iranian who disagrees with you.

And until that distinction becomes clear, the regime's greatest advantage may not be its strength.

It may be the opposition's inability to get out of its own way.

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

Here's the latest Netflix news as of mid-January 2026!

The streaming giant is kicking off the year strong with a packed slate of new releases, ongoing buzz around major deals, and continued subscriber growth.

Major Highlights

Netflix is reportedly in the midst of a blockbuster acquisition: the company has agreed to buy Warner Bros. in a massive deal valued at around $82.7 billion (with some reports citing $72 billion in equity value).

This move aims to supercharge its content library with iconic franchises like Harry Potter and classic films.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

text:
WEIRD ANIMAL FACTS
A Shark Attack at Lake Michigan

Sprawled out through the U.S. states of Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan is the majestic Lake Michigan, one of Great Lakes of North America, and at a size roughly slightly larger than the state of Virginia it is the second largest of these giants. A wondrous and vast body of water known for its generous beachfront, earning it the nickname of America’s “Third Coast,” Lake Michigan draws in all manner of tourists and locals looking to engage in the various recreational activities the lake has to offer. While this “Third Coast” might sport beautiful beaches and water sports, one would think that this would be the last place to find sharks, but surprisingly there have been reports of these creatures lurking in the depths here, and even at least one attack.

According to the 1975 book Man Eating Sharks! by Felix Dennis, on a beautiful, clear summer day in 1955, one beach along the shores of Lake Michigan was packed with people looking to cool off and enjoy the sunny day, and one of these was George Lawson, a boy from Chicago. Lawson was out with many others splashing about and swimming off a boat near the beach when witnesses allegedly saw him pulled underwater, seemingly by something yanking him under and accompanied by the boy’s panicked screams. Shockingly, a dorsal fin was reported by several others on the boat as cutting away through the water right after the incident.

One man named John Adler managed to reach the thrashing boy and pull him aboard the boat, where it was found that the victim was entirely missing one of his legs below the knee. Adler would say of his thoughts as Lawson writhed about and the pool of blood spread in front of stunned witnesses, “I just couldn’t believe it, but I had to believe what I saw happening right before my eyes!” Lawson was rushed to the hospital, where doctors apparently were quick to recognize the bite wound as having been inflicted by a shark.

This was understandably rather shocking, as this had been in a freshwater lake well inland and nowhere near the ocean. However, it was ascertained that it had perhaps been a bull shark that had made its way up to the lake by way of the Illinois River. This is actually not impossible, as bull sharks are well-known for their spooky ability to easily acclimate to freshwater, tolerating it for long periods and in some cases indefinitely, and they are definitely aggressive, blamed for all manner of attacks on humans. While it would have been quite a distance to travel for a bull shark, there have been reports of these creatures making their way hundreds of miles inland through river systems. For instance, bull sharks have been found up the Mississippi River as far as Illinois, Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Indeed, in September of 1937, two fishermen named "Dudge" Collins and Herbert Copes began to notice that something was ransacking and damaging their fish traps in the Mississippi River near Alton, Illinois. They at first guessed that it was a particularly massive catfish, and went about trying to catch it in a seine net. The plan worked, and they began to haul up something very large and very pissed off, but rather than the granddaddy catfish they expected to pull up instead they found it to be a bull shark that measured over five-feet long and weighed 84 pounds, thrashing and biting rather threateningly. Besides the extreme distance from the ocean, authorities insisted that the dam system at Alton should have kept any bull shark from reaching the area, making its presence there very mysterious indeed.

Bull sharks have even been known to brave the extraordinarily the frigid waters of these northern locales. In the autumn of 2005 shark teeth were found along the Minnehaha creek, a very cold creek not far from the city of Minneapolis, Minnesota, which were analyzed and found to be those of a juvenile bull shark and dated as being very recent. When officials went about using electric shocks to stun the river fish of the area in an effort to find any sharks in the creek they were stunned themselves to capture two healthy juvenile bull sharks that had been lurking there alive and well. The sharks were apparently then sent to the Minnesota zoo and survived the ordeal. The whole incident would cause the creek to be closed off to swimming, just in case.

In February of that next year, a truck fell through the ice of Lake Pepin, which is more or less just a wide area of the Mississippi between Wisconsin and Minnesota. While the driver survived unharmed, salvage divers who went to in investigate the sunken vehicle got quite a fright when they discovered a full grown 5-foot long bull shark taking refuge in the wreck, lurking there in the murk. It was weak and dying from the cold, but it was still very much alive, and no doubt a frightening sight to see ensconced there at the bottom of a lake within this sunken hull. Interestingly, there is a lake monster said to prowl Lake Pepin, the has been affectionately called “Pepie,” so one wonders if sharks are to blame for this phenomenon.

Coming back to Lake Michigan, it is incredible that there was yet another shark report in the days after this event. Anglers Gil Scharnek and Cal Lukasavitz were reportedly out on the lake one day when they spied what they at first thought to be a piece of debris or flotsam. A seagull had been perched upon it and alighted when the men approached, revealing something altogether stranger. As they approached they could see that it was some type of shark, and they collected it to put it on ice. Later analysis showed that it was a blacktip shark, which is very odd since not only is the lake far from their habitat, but they have no known tolerance for fresh water. Curious indeed. In recent years there was even recent video footage taken of a supposed shark in Lake Michigan near a place called McKinley beach. Is it real or fake?

This all seems to show that this attack in Lake Michigan is at least plausible, but did it ever really happen? Was this shark attack of 1955 real or just a hoax and piece of "fake news"? It seems that in this day and age the dams and levees leading up to the lake would prevent something so sinister from creeping in, but has there ever been a shark or sharks prowling Lake Michigan and if so are they still there? At this point no one really knows.

text:
Ads Turned Into Spyware: Israel’s Discover‑Tech hijacks global ad networks for surveillance.

From Clickbait to Cyberwar: How ad‑tech became Mossad’s new battlefield.

Occupation by Algorithm: Palestine flooded with weaponized ads in covert intelligence blitz.

So, the mask slips again. The latest investigation into Discover‑Tech shows what many already suspected: Israel’s intelligence ecosystem has fused seamlessly with the global advertising machine. Forget the tired clichés about “start‑up nation” innovation — this is surveillance capitalism weaponized, with a military‑industrial accent.

The Banality of Spyware

Citizen Lab and Confiant’s findings are damning: spyware delivered through online ads, no clicks required, no dodgy pop‑ups, just the invisible plumbing of the internet turned into a weapon. They even gave it a catchy name — AdFection — as if it were a new dating app. The banality is the point: surveillance doesn’t need to look sinister anymore. It’s embedded in the same infrastructure that sells you trainers and streaming subscriptions.

Israel’s Cyber Doctrine in Action

This isn’t a rogue company gone astray. It’s the logical extension of Unit 8200 doctrine: pre‑emptive surveillance, precision targeting, and plausible deniability through “private firms.” Discover‑Tech, Candiru, NSO — they’re not startups, they’re subcontractors in a state‑directed cyber war. The fact that Candiru had to rebrand as “Integrity Labs” is almost parody: integrity is the last thing on offer.

Journalism as Target Practice

Al Jazeera staff were among those infected. That’s not collateral damage, it’s deliberate. Journalists are treated as combatants in the information battlespace. Israel’s spyware industry has long been accused of undermining press freedom, but this case is particularly brazen: turning ad slots into sniper scopes. Al Jazeera called it an “assault on press freedom.” They’re right — but it’s also an assault on the very idea that digital infrastructure can be neutral.

Palestine Saturated

The geographic data is telling: Palestine was flooded with Discover‑Tech ads, peaking at nearly 10% of all impressions on April 7. That’s not commercial targeting, that’s occupation logic translated into code. Surveillance saturation as a digital extension of territorial control. The ad exchange becomes another checkpoint, another watchtower, another layer of domination.

Global Spillover

Belgium, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain — all lit up on the radar. This isn’t just about Palestine or Al Jazeera. It’s about proving that ad‑tech can be hijacked anywhere, anytime. The platforms involved — Google, Yandex, Beeswax — are global. The message is clear: if Israel can weaponize them, so can anyone else. The infrastructure is rotten, and the rot is systemic.

The Illusion of Consent

EU privacy rules? Forget it. Discover‑Tech harvested device fingerprints, IPs, cookies, authentication tokens — all without consent. The GDPR looks laughably toothless in the face of this kind of operation. Regulators are still stuck debating cookie banners while spyware rides the ad rails straight into your phone.

Surveillance Capitalism Meets Military Occupation

This is the real story: the fusion of commercial ad‑tech with military intelligence. Shoshana Zuboff warned about surveillance capitalism, but here it’s not just about selling products — it’s about selling control. The same infrastructure that tracks your shopping habits can track dissidents, journalists, even heads of government. The line between consumer profiling and counter‑insurgency has evaporated.

Bottom Line 

Strip away the technical jargon and what you see is a grotesque parody of “innovation.” Israel’s cyber‑industrial complex has taken the most banal feature of modern capitalism — online ads — and turned it into a weapon of war. It’s not just dystopian, it’s depressingly predictable. When you build a global system designed to commodify attention and harvest data, of course it becomes a playground for intelligence agencies.  

The Western press will wring its hands, regulators will issue stern statements, and nothing will change. Because the ad‑tech industry is too profitable, too entrenched, too useful to power. Discover‑Tech is just the latest Frankenstein’s monster stitched together from venture capital, military doctrine, and Silicon Valley infrastructure. And like every Frankenstein, it’s already out of control.

text:
It remains a considerable shame that Timothy Dalton was denied a third film as James Bond.

Dalton's Bond was lean, almost lupine, and the menace resided entirely in the man himself. A certain stillness, the controlled intensity of the voice, the way his eyes could harden in an instant, those were his weapons. He could radiate a cold, professional ruthlessness that felt entirely authentic, the sort of quiet lethality one associates with the literary Bond of Ian Fleming's novels. Crucially, he could switch off the coldness. There was charm there, a capacity for warmth that made the ruthlessness more potent by contrast. One never doubted that this was a man who killed when required and who was equally capable of being a civilised gentleman when the Walther was holstered.

Dalton's classical training showed to his advantage. The stage-honed ability to modulate presence, to hold a scene with little more than phrasing and stillness, suited the character of Bond perfectly. The danger from him was intellectual and psychological as much as it was kinetic. In that respect he was, to my mind, the closest we have come to Fleming's original conception: the professional secret agent living on the edge, capable of being both refined and feral, not a superhero but a thoroughly dangerous man.

The third film that might have completed the portrait was already taking shape when circumstances intervened. By the spring of 1990, Michael G. Wilson and Alfonse Ruggiero had completed a detailed outline treatment for Dalton's third Bond. It opened with a catastrophic explosion at a chemical weapons laboratory in Scotland, set off when robotic devices ran amok. The principal antagonist was Sir Henry Lee Ching, a brilliant, thirty-year-old British-Chinese entrepreneur and electronics prodigy of distinctly unsound mind. His scheme turned on a computer virus capable of paralysing military and commercial systems worldwide, with the approaching handover of Hong Kong supplying both motive and setting. The action would have carried Bond through Hong Kong, Japan and mainland China, culminating in a Die Hard-style confrontation inside Sir Henry's hi-tech high-rise, which Bond would enter via the sewers and waste-pipe before dispatching the villain with a welding torch to the face. The intention was to retain the grounded ruthlessness of Licence to Kill while introducing more ambitious technological spectacle. Dalton later recalled that a script existed which he regarded as "quite a good story," one he would have been enthusiastic to make into "a real scorcher" that synthesised the best of his two completed films. Directors were being interviewed, and the production was advancing when the legal difficulties froze everything.

Those difficulties arose after Licence to Kill, when MGM/United Artists, already in financial straits, was being acquired by Pathé Communications under Giancarlo Parretti. To finance the purchase, Parretti proposed to sell off television and home-video rights to the studio's catalogue at sharply reduced rates; the Bond films, still the most valuable asset, were included. Danjaq, the Broccoli family's holding company that owns the 007 rights, sued on the grounds that the proposed sales violated the long-standing distribution agreements originally struck with United Artists in the 1960s. Countersuits followed, and the litigation dragged on, bringing all production to a halt. By the time the matter was settled, Dalton's original contract had expired. He initially indicated he did not see himself continuing. Later, he reconsidered and offered to return for a single picture that would consolidate the strongest elements of The Living Daylights and Licence to Kill. The producers, after a five-year gap, insisted he commit to four or five further films. Dalton judged that "too much, too long" and declined.

It is a shame because, in my honest opinion, he was the quintessential James Bond.

#TimothyDalton #JamesBond #TheLivingDaylights #LicencetoKill

text:
Tonight's film is the sixteenth James Bond film, Licence to Kill.

I feel compelled to remind those who declare Daniel Craig's Bond to be the darkest and most realistic that this film exists and does a better job of gritty realism than all five of Craig's films. This film is not everyone’s favourite, yet it is one that remembers a tradition that modern cinema has largely forgotten: villains must meet endings that are not merely fatal but fittingly severe.

The current tendency toward clean, almost anti-climactic endings leaves the spectator with the sense that the monster has not been fittingly punished. Licence to Kill delivers satisfaction in the demise of its villain, Franz Sanchez, portrayed by Robert Davi.

From Dr. No's immersion in reactor coolant in 1962 to Sanchez's immolation in 1989's Licence to Kill, the James Bond films understand that certain villains forfeit the ordinary mercy of an anti-climax. Sanchez is not simply defeated. The petrol, the lighter, and the final remark to him are not gratuitous; they are a moral symmetry. He is dealt with in the same brutal way in which he himself dealt with others.

Robert Brown's M operates within a more formal administrative framework than Bernard Lee's. The latter, one suspects, would have granted Bond a quiet fortnight's leave to "sort it out." The former revokes Bond's licence. This is one of the reasons why I remain convinced that Brown's M is Admiral Hargreaves, first introduced in The Spy Who Loved Me.

There is no contradiction in Bond's brutality in this film. The mention of his ill-fated marriage serves precisely to remind us that his professionalism has been set aside for the pursuit of revenge before. The same man who methodically pursued Blofeld after Tracy's death would, upon the mutilation of so close a friend as Felix Leiter, set the Service aside for vengeance. Licence to Kill merely shows, in a darker register, what we have already seen: that Bond can switch off his charm and can punish the villain with a brutal final moment.

It remains a shame that Dalton was not given further films in which to explore the aftermath of that decision. His successor, Pierce Brosnan, to his credit, continued the tradition of granting the villains spectacularly bad endings.

This film does not merely gesture toward grittiness; it commits to it with an entertaining severity that the Craig cycle only intermittently approached, and then often with poor pacing and a self-conscious overlay that Licence to Kill largely forgoes. They don't make them like this anymore.

For this reason, I consider Licence to Kill to be the most underrated Bond film.

#JamesBond #TimothyDalton #LicencetoKill #RobertDavi

text:
There is a particular quality of credibility in the villains of John Glen's Bond films that the series has seldom matched. They are not, for the most part, men who seek to rule the world. They are smugglers, defectors, assassins, and dealers who exploit the fractures of their moment, arms, drugs, and double-crosses.

In The Living Daylights, Georgi Koskov, portrayed by Jeroen Krabbé, is a cultured, smiling KGB general whose treachery is motivated by pecuniary interest. Brad Whitaker, portrayed by Joe Don Baker, is a boastful American arms dealer with a museum of statues that look like him, serving as the emblem of a grotesque kind of vanity, and a plan that turns on diamonds and opium. Necros, portrayed by Andreas Wisniewski, is simply a professional assassin. None of them require a monologue about the end of civilisation or world domination; their motives are limited to money, and one can easily picture such men existing.

Glen's earlier pictures with Sir Roger Moore already leaned this way after the excesses of Moonraker. For Your Eyes Only prefers smugglers and double-dealers to megalomaniacs; even his final film Licence to Kill treats its drug baron as a ruthless territorial gangster rather than megalomaniacal genius. 

Sir Roger himself, after watching the film, called The Living Daylights a bloody good film. High praise from the man who had carried the role of 007 with such effortless charm. Dalton's colder Bond fitted Glen's approach exactly: the menace is sold by the presence of the actor and not by visual effect. Contemporary films have largely forgotten how to do this.

#TheLivingDaylights #JohnGlen #JamesBond #TimothyDalton

text:
The interpretations are already arriving, frequently with the assurance of people who appear to know exactly what today means before today has even ended. I have no desire to contribute another one.

France is taking place inside a world that has offered almost no opportunity to absorb one development before the next arrives. Students and police have clashed in Brussels. The unrest in Tirana has entered another day of confrontations, arrests, and demands for political change. Demonstrations over housing and living costs continue appearing across parts of Europe, each with its own immediate causes, histories, grievances, and participants. The war in Ukraine continues while the relationship between Washington and Kyiv deteriorates over Russian sanctions, energy supplies, and the conduct of the war itself. The easing of American economic pressure on Moscow has provoked criticism from Ukraine and within the United States, while the attacks on infrastructure and the uncertainty surrounding future assistance continue. Across the Middle East, reports arrive of diplomats attacked in the occupied West Bank, violence surrounding the olive harvest, deaths in Gaza and Yemen, vessels attacked near the Persian Gulf, and the continuing vulnerability of commercial aviation and energy infrastructure across the region. Behind each headline are lives that continue long after the headline disappears, people who will not be afforded the luxury of deciding whether the events deserve their attention. Meanwhile, financial markets have just completed another severe week for technology shares, with the Nasdaq falling approximately 4.5 percent over five sessions and the enormous expectations surrounding artificial intelligence encountering renewed questions about financing, energy costs, valuations, and the returns on an infrastructure expansion whose scale has few historical comparisons. The markets are closed tonight. The wars are not. The demonstrations continue into the evening. The world is producing more information than any individual can absorb, and the machinery through which that information is delivered remains almost entirely indifferent to the difference between knowing that something has happened and understanding what has happened.

Washington's foreign policy geniuses are still obsessing over Trump's Greenland rhetoric while he attempts to assemble something considerably more consequential: a network of military access, energy infrastructure, and commercial relationships stretching across the Western Hemisphere.

And these smug bastards are so busy critiquing his delivery they're barely examining the strategy.

Start with Greenland.

A reported military-access arrangement involving Denmark and Greenland, followed by preparations for expanded oil, gas, and mineral exploration. Arctic security creates opportunities for investment. Investment creates economic interests. Those interests give future governments reasons to preserve the security relationship.

Now move to Alaska.

Trump has announced a proposed twenty-year agreement for Taiwan to purchase 30 percent of the natural gas from a new pipeline, alongside billions in potential Asian investment.

American resources. Foreign capital. Infrastructure designed to operate across administrations.

Every year that pipeline operates would deepen commercial relationships that future presidents inherit rather than negotiate from scratch.

Then look south.

Venezuela's energy resources offer another opportunity to expand American commercial influence, strengthen energy relationships, and establish leverage in a region where outside powers have pursued their own strategic interests for years.

See the pattern?

Military access supports investment. Investment supports infrastructure. Infrastructure creates economic dependence and enduring strategic relationships.

Each component reinforces the others.

And while Trump pursues that architecture, the diplomatic establishment is practically hyperventilating over international norms and whether he properly respects Europe's delicate fucking sensibilities.

What an extraordinary collection of credentialed fools.

These people can spend six months debating the implications of a presidential adjective while an entirely different geopolitical arrangement begins taking shape beneath their noses.

The projects still require execution. Agreements must hold. Capital must arrive. Infrastructure must be built.

But the potential structure is unmistakable: American influence reinforced by economic interests powerful enough to survive changes in political leadership.

That's the kind of strategic thinking Washington supposedly pays its foreign policy establishment to understand.

Instead, they're treating the Greenland discussion like an endless argument over Trump's manners.

Imagine spending your career claiming to understand global power, then becoming so consumed with mocking the opening move that you fail to notice the board changing.

Washington is still arguing about Greenland.

Trump is trying to redraw the fucking map.

They RESCINDED the entire offer.

And then employers wonder why workers have no trust in the hiring process.

Imagine spending years trying to get hired, finally getting an offer, and learning that even politely asking for a little more money can cost you the entire opportunity.

Apparently, companies are desperate for workers until a worker dares to ask what their labor is actually worth.

text:
Anthropic has signed about $530B of data center leases. @theinformation says the rush is because every month a 245 MW Louisiana site energizes early is worth ~$1.3B. That makes grid power the prize. I priced the leases. Thread.

The claim: ~$1.3B a month of revenue on that site, ~$200M a month to rent the chips, ~85% gross margin. @AnthropicAI Q3: $16.8B revenue, up 45%, with $1.70 of revenue per compute dollar. That implies a company-wide compute margin near 41%, not 85%.

Now price the power. Hut 8's River Bend lease: $7.0B, 15 years, 245 MW, about $1.9M per MW-year. TeraWulf's Kentucky lease to Anthropic: about $19B, 20 years, ~401 MW, about $2.4M per MW-year.

The article's own math implies $63.7M of revenue per usable MW-year (implied, not reported). Facility rent is 3.0% of that at Hut 8 and 3.7% at TeraWulf. If power were the scarce thing, the landlords sold it cheap.

Where the big checks go: a $125.2B five-year TPU lease. Broadcom lending up to $42B against $23.975B of its reported cash. A ~$60B TPU package that reportedly offered Blackstone a 10% coupon. Leverage sits with silicon and capital.

The exception: where power is missing, everything slips. Nscale's Norway grid expansion isn't expected much before 2037. And ready capacity costs the most: SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 is $1.25B a month for 300 MW, ~$50M per MW-year, on 90 days' notice.

Numbers that disagree: River Bend's first hall is Q2 2027 (Hut 8), Q1 2027 (Axios), end of 2027 (WAFB). Commitments: $530B (The Information), $518B (Reuters), $417B (different basis). Nobody has explained the $12B gap.

My read: the sprint can be rational, but 85% is a site number and the company-level compute margin is ~41%. Power access decides who can build; chips and debt decide how fast. Full dispatch:

text:
110,550 swing seats sold on Amazon were just recalled.
They're PACEARTH U-type swing seats, sold from May 2017 through June 2026 for $27 to $57.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission says the seat, the carabiners or quick links, or the webbing straps can break during use.
The seller has at least 30 reports of falls and at least nine injuries.
The remedy is a full refund.
To get it, you write "RECALLED" on the seat in permanent marker and email the company a photo.

If someone in your house fell from one, slow down before you grab the marker.
A recall refund pays you back for the product.
An injury claim is a separate matter, and the recall notice offers only the refund.
→ Stop using the swing either way.
→ After a fall, keep the seat, the hardware and the order record.
→ You can report it to the CPSC through its SaferProducts site.
The broken part is the evidence.

Deadlines keep running, recall or no recall.
In Oklahoma, 12 O.S. 95 gives two years for most injury claims.
Other states set their own clocks.
At our firm, the first thing I'd ask is where the swing is right now.
P.S. Look up CPSC recall number 27-019. The recalled swings have chains coated in yellow plastic.
P.P.S. Edutainment based on a real recall notice and public reporting. It isn't formal legal advice.

text:
8.78 Miles.That's the difference between paying $17.75 more for one set of lights or my in case $17.75 X 6 = $106.50.

That's the tip of the iceberg when it comes to @HomeDepot Customer Service. I found the lights I wanted at the Home Depot website. It offered the option of delivery; but, then I saw them in-store 8.78 miles away, so I thought, " Man, I can start working on my project tomorrow. Why don't I go & pick them up?" 

Upon driving 25 minutes (Houston), I get there & am startled to find that the price was not what I saw online. I asked to do a price check & surely it was $53. I, then, speak to a lady who said, "Oh yea, you have to change the store to the one your purchasing from on the website." I stand there, face getting red, speechless. "You want to know why? she asked." No, I'm not interested because I know the reason. Your scumbag eCommerce Team thought it was a great idea to jerk around customers all over f**king town for $17.75 & told you not to match prices 8.78 Miles away. 

I get back home 25 minutes later, begrudgingly shaking my head, as I go upstairs to battle their online purchasing system. I attempt to order via Delivery; but keep getting the message, "The quantity requested is no longer available for Scheduled Delivery for some of these items." I could not continue forward with my cart; so I decide (against my better judgment) to call Customer Service. 

YES!!!! Foreign accent. Just what I wanted to deal with on a Saturday night. After struggling to understand for five minutes, she basically said the system couldn't obtain an accurate count for delivery at my local store & couldn't provide me a time when it would be resolved. I just hung up.

I had to partition my order for partial pick-up at the store that I ALREADY traveled to (different length of lights not available for store delivery) & In-store delivery for Wednesday.

After all this time, I just agreed. I pocketed the $106.50 plus tax & wasted an entire evening wasting my time.

This is where we are as a service economy, slaves to systems that made us less customer centric, efficient, & personal. 

All of this sucks. Every little bit of it.

text:
Export Exchange 2026, sponsored by the U.S. Grains & BioProducts Council, Growth Energy and the Renewable Fuels Association, concluded Saturday with a focus on new products, sustainability and the superior value of U.S. corn.

Export Exchange is a biannual event allowing buyers and sellers of U.S. corn, distiller’s dried grains with solubles, sorghum and other commodities to network and gain a better understanding of the needs of buyers around the world and the caliber of supply the U.S. provides.

Speakers during the last day of the event illustrated numerous reasons why U.S. commodities offer the best advantage to global buyers and how its scalable and transparent export system provides direct access to satisfy grain needs around the world.

“Whether you’re heading home or out to see the U.S. value chain up close in one of our partner states, we appreciate you spending time getting to know the U.S. commodities we are so proud of. We hope you leave us with no doubt that superiority of U.S. products is just that... superior,” said Ryan LeGrand, USGBC president and CEO.

"This edition of Export Exchange shattered previous records with more than 500 attendees from 48 countries. Your participation demonstrates international understanding of the level of service you get when you buy U.S. grains and their co-products."

Additional concluding presentations included a dive into details about new co-products in the market by Distillers Technology Council Executive Director Joe Ward; a look into how the U.S. Department of Agriculture works to expand U.S. agricultural exports with USDA International Trade Specialist Collin Bradley; and a panel discussion about U.S. corn’s superior performance and value moderated by USGBC Manager of Global Strategies and Trade Mark Sevier.

Thirteen trade teams visited key corn value chain stakeholders prior to Export Exchange, and at the conclusion of the conference seven more groups will head out across the country to observe farming operations, explore DDGS production at ethanol plants, view port facilities and more to build their networks with U.S. suppliers.

These groups include:
Bangladesh: heading to North Dakota, Oct. 18-21
China: heading to Texas, Oct. 18-21
China and Mongolia: heading to Kansas, Oct. 18-21
Latin America: heading to Ohio, Oct. 18-21
South Korea: heading to Minnesota, Oct. 18-21
Southeast Asia: heading to Nebraska, Oct. 18-21
Southeast Asia: heading to Indiana, Oct. 18-21

More information is available at https://t.co/yUxMZCbeVa or on social media at #ExEx26.

text:
🇺🇸 Why Americans May Choose Trump-Aligned Republicans in the 2026 Midterms
Political analysis | October 18, 2026
Trump himself is not on the ballot. Americans will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and approximately one-third of the Senate.
Seven arguments Republican supporters emphasize
1. Economic growth and prosperity. Republicans advocate lower taxes, deregulation, private investment and business expansion as ways to encourage growth.
2. American energy independence. Trump supports expanded domestic oil and natural gas production, fewer restrictions on fossil-fuel development and lower energy costs.
3. Border security and immigration enforcement. Republicans emphasize stronger border controls, immigration-law enforcement and restrictions on unauthorized immigration.
4. American manufacturing and employment. Trump advocates tariffs, domestic production and policies designed to encourage companies to invest in the United States.
5. National security and military strength. Republicans emphasize military readiness, deterrence, American strategic interests and greater defense contributions from allies.
6. Traditional conservative values. Many Republican candidates emphasize religious liberty, parental authority, gun rights and conservative judicial appointments.
7. Continuity of government policy. A Republican congressional majority could make it easier for Trump to advance legislation, confirm nominees in the Senate and maintain support for his administration's priorities.
These are arguments made by supporters, not guarantees of particular economic or political outcomes.
What voters should also consider
The economic results remain contested. Recent reporting highlights inflation, high energy prices, concerns about tariffs and disagreements over immigration enforcement. 
A Pew Research Center survey conducted September 28–October 4 found:
Economy 84%
Future of democracy 73%
Immigration 59%
Share of U.S. registered voters describing each issue as very important to their midterm vote. 
The central choice
For voters who agree with Trump's policy direction, Republican congressional candidates offer the possibility of greater legislative continuity. For voters who disagree, Democratic candidates offer an alternative policy direction and stronger congressional oversight of the administration.
The fundamental question of the 2026 midterms is what direction Americans want Congress to take during the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.
The decision ultimately rests on each candidate's record, proposals and ability to deliver measurable results.
